10:5: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i.C Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division—Procedure</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:5</designator><name date.updated="0">Appeal Hearing: Sequence of Events</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">At the hearing, the appellant first testifies and gives evidence in support of his or her appeal. If counsel is present, this evidence is elicited through counsel's direct examination. The Minister's counsel then cross-examines the appellant on the evidence given at the hearing. During or following either the direct examination and cross-examination, the decision-maker, an IAD Member, may also question the appellant and any witnesses. Following the appellant's testimony, the witnesses testify. This may include the appellant's witnesses as well as any witnesses that the Minister produces. After the appellant and the witnesses have testified, the IAD member will ask the appellant or the appellant's counsel to make submissions in support of the appeal. The Minister's counsel will then make submissions, to which the appellant will be given an opportunity to reply.<footnote date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">0.50</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, “Step 6: Attend your hearing”, 16 January 2023, online: <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="I23464be07a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45">https://irb.gc.ca/en/making-immigration-appeal/Pages/immapp-e7.aspx</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">At the close of the hearing, the IAD Member may give a decision either with or without reasons. More often, however, the Member will <?WGXPPrightHandPageStart releaseDate="2023;12;31" sp=";;7" folio="10-7" releaseNumber="4" hyphenated="n" nep=";;27" backBlank="n" backFolio="10-8" ?>reserve his or her decision and reasons will be sent to the appellant by mail at a later date, usually no later than 60 days after the hearing.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124"><para.text date.updated="0">Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, “Step 7: Receive the decision”, 16 January 2023, online: <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="I23464be17a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45">https://irb.gc.ca/en/making-immigration-appeal/Pages/immapp-e8.aspx</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:6: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i.D Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division—Evidence</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:6</designator><name date.updated="0">Evidence</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Appellants should bear in mind that they are not confined to any formal rules of evidence when they appear before the IAD, as set out under s. 175 (above) of the <ital>IRPA</ital>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The assessment of the evidence should be framed in terms of its credibility and trustworthiness, as that is the test set out in the Act. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>IRPA</ital>, S.C. 2001, c. 27.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:7: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:7</designator><name date.updated="0">Introduction</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Pursuant to s. 66 of the <ital>IRPA</ital>, the IAD member may make one of the following orders in a removal order appeal: allow the appeal, stay the removal order, or dismiss the appeal.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:8: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i.C Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division—Procedure</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:8</designator><name date.updated="0">Allow the Appeal</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Pursuant to s. 67(1) of the <ital>IRPA</ital>, in order for the IAD to allow an appeal it must be satisfied that either:</para.text><list list.style="para" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(<ital>a</ital>)</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>the decision appealed is wrong in law or fact or mixed law and fact;</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(<ital>b</ital>)</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>a principle of natural justice has not been observed; or</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(<ital>c</ital>)</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>other than in the case of an appeal by the Minister, taking into account the best interests of a child directly affected by the decision, sufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations warrant special relief in light of all the circumstances of the case.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">If the appeal is allowed, the decision is set aside and either a new decision is rendered or the matter is referred to a decision-maker for reconsideration pursuant to s. 67(2) of the <ital>IRPA</ital>, which states:</para.text><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">67.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="yeswithspace" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.trace="20210811" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(2)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="20231124"><bold>If the Immigration Appeal Division allows the appeal, it shall set aside the original decision and substitute a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made, including the making of a removal order, or refer the matter to the appropriate decision-maker for reconsideration.</bold></stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.section></stat.structure></para></section.body></section>
10:9: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.f.iii Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Removal orders—Stay of execution</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:9</designator><name date.updated="0">Stay of Removal Order</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">If the removal order is stayed, the person concerned can remain in Canada for a specified period of time and under certain conditions imposed by the IAD. Section 68 of the <ital>IRPA</ital> specifies that in order to stay a removal order, the IAD must be satisfied, taking into account the best interests of a child directly affected by the decision, that sufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations warrant special relief in light of all the circumstances of the case. The humanitarian and compassionate factors that are typically considered by the IAD are set out in the case of <ital>Ribic</ital>, <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ribic" p2="Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration)" post.rptr="1357" pre.rptr="1986" ref.id="I94b92ac09b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Ribic v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration)">Ribic v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration) (1986), 1986 CarswellNat 1357, [1985] I.A.D.D. No. 4 (Imm. App. Bd.)</ref></cite>. In <ital>Ribic</ital>, the IAD set out factors to be considered in the exercise of its discretion, as endorsed by the Supreme Court of Canada in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref date="2002" p1="Chieu" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)" post.rptr="3" pre.rptr="2002" ref.id="I2347ab707a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45" title="Chieu v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)">Chieu v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2002 SCC 3, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 84 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite> at paras. 40, 41, 90: “(1) the seriousness of the offence leading to the removal order; (2) the possibility of rehabilitation; (3) the length of time spent, and the degree to which the individual facing removal is established in Canada; (4) the family and community support available to the individual facing removal; (5) the family in Canada and the dislocation to the family that removal would cause; and (6) the degree of hardship that would be caused to the individual facing removal to their country of nationality.”</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> discussed in detail below. Section 68(2)(a) of the <ital>IRPA</ital> states that the IAD <ital>shall</ital> impose any condition that is prescribed and <ital>may</ital> impose any condition that it considers necessary.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:10: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.f.iii Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Removal orders—Stay of execution</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:10</designator><name date.updated="0">Stay of Removal Order<sep/>Mandatory Conditions</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The mandatory conditions that must be placed on a stay are set out at s. 251 of the <ital>Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations</ital> (“<ital>IRPR</ital>”):</para.text><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.trace="20210811" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">251.</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="yeswithspace" date.updated="0"><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>For the purposes of subsection 68(2) of the Act, the conditions that must be imposed on a foreign national or permanent resident by the Immigration Appeal Division are the following:</bold></stat.text><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(<ital>a</ital>)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>to inform the Canada Border Services Agency and the Immigration Appeal Division in writing, in advance, of any change in their address;</bold></stat.text></stat.para><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(<ital>b</ital>)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>to provide to the Canada Border Services Agency a copy of any passport and travel document that they hold and, if they do not hold any such documents, to complete an application for a passport or travel document and provide that application to the Agency;</bold></stat.text></stat.para><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(<ital>c</ital>)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>to apply for an extension of the validity period of any passport and travel document that they hold before it expires and to provide a copy of the extended document to the Canada Border Services Agency;</bold></stat.text></stat.para><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(<ital>d</ital>)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>to not commit an offence under an Act of Parliament or an offence that, if committed in Canada, would constitute an offence under an Act of Parliament;</bold></stat.text></stat.para><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(<ital>e</ital>)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>if they are charged with an offence under an Act of Parliament or an offence that, if committed in Canada, would constitute an offence under an Act of Parliament, to inform the Canada Border Services Agency of that charge in writing and without delay; and</bold></stat.text></stat.para><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(<ital>f</ital>)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>if they are convicted of an offence under an Act of Parliament or an offence that, if committed in Canada, would constitute an offence under an Act of Parliament, to inform the Canada Border Services Agency and the Immigration Appeal Division of that conviction in writing and without delay.</bold></stat.text></stat.para></stat.subsect></stat.section></stat.structure></para></section.body></section>
10:11: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.f.iii Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Removal orders—Stay of execution</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:11</designator><name date.updated="0">Stay of Removal Order<sep/>Discretionary Conditions</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Discretionary conditions depend on the nature of the appellant's situation and are established during the hearing before the IAD. They can be suggested by the Minister's counsel and the appellant, but ultimately, the IAD Member decides which conditions will be imposed. Conditions of a stay of removal that are frequently imposed by the IAD in criminal inadmissibility appeals include the following:</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">1</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Report to the CBSA on the dates set by the IAD. Reporting may be in person, in writing or by telephone;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">2</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Certain living arrangements;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">3</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Attendance at meetings of Alcoholics Anonymous or any other drug or alcohol rehabilitation program;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">4</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Reasonable efforts to seek and maintain full-time employment and report any change in employment to the CBSA;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">5</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Attendance at any educational instruction, or any changes to that attendance;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124" toc.include="y"><designator date.updated="0">6</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Not knowingly associate with individuals who have a criminal record or who are engaged in criminal activity, except contact that might result while attending meetings of Alcoholics Anonymous, or any other drug or alcohol rehabilitation program;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124" toc.include="y"><designator date.updated="0">7</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Not own or possess offensive weapons or imitations of offensive weapons;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124" toc.include="y"><designator date.updated="0">8</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Respect all parole conditions and any court orders;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124" toc.include="y"><designator date.updated="0">9</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Refrain from the use of alcohol;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124" toc.include="y"><designator date.updated="0">10</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Keep the peace and be of good behaviour; <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">We note that in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Huynh" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)" post.rptr="1426" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I94b978e09b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Huynh v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)">Huynh v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2003 FC 1426 (F.C.)</ref></cite>, Justice O'Reilly considered the meaning of a stay condition requiring the applicant to be of “good behaviour”. He found that to be of “good behaviour”, one must abide by federal, provincial or municipal statutes and regulations. <ital>Huynh</ital> was cited with approval by Justice Mactavish in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cooper" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)" post.rptr="1253" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I94b978e19b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Cooper v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)">Cooper v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2005 FC 1253 (F.C.)</ref></cite>. In <ital>Cooper</ital>, the issue before the Court was whether the applicant's convictions in relation to provincial automobile offences constituted a breach of the condition of the stay of his deportation requiring him to “keep the peace and be of good behaviour and not commit further criminal offences”. The Court found that it was indeed a breach of this condition. However, the IAD's decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cao" p2="Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness)" post.rptr="5196" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I94b978e29b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Cao v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness)">Cao v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness), 2006 CarswellNat 5196, [2006] I.A.D.D. No. 101 (Imm. & Ref. Bd. (App. Div.))</ref></cite> and the Federal Court's decision in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Avalos" p2="Canada (Ministre de la Citoyenneté & de l'Immigration)" post.rptr="830" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I94b978e39b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Avalos c. Canada (Ministre de la Citoyenneté & de l'Immigration)">Avalos c. Canada (Ministre de la Citoyenneté & de l'Immigration), 2005 FC 830 (F.C.)</ref></cite> stand for the position that the Board is not prevented from considering any reasonable explanation relating to the breach of the condition to “keep the peace and be of good behaviour”, and that a determination as to whether a breach has taken place must be made in the context of evidence and arguments on this specific issue. Mr. Justice Campbell judicially affirmed the reasonableness of the approach taken by the Board in <ital>Cao</ital> in the case of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness)" p2="Ali" post.rptr="431" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I94b978e49b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness) v. Ali">Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness) v. Ali, 2008 FC 431 (F.C.)</ref></cite>. In <ital>Ali</ital>, Justice Campbell as then was, also affirmed the principle that an analysis of whether a person has breached the condition to be of “good behaviour,” a person's general conduct is an important factor. If there is a contravention of a statute or regulatory measure, <ital>“the opportunity is triggered to evaluate whether that contravention results in a further finding that a breach of ‘good behaviour’ has occurred”</ital> (see <ital>Ali</ital> at par. 5.).</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">11</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124">Participation in psychotherapy or counselling of a specific type;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">12</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Refrain from the illegal use or sale of drugs.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">2</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Rubinoff, Joel. “Chapter 10 – Remedies & Conditions of a Stay, In Removal Order Appeals”, 1 January 2009, online: <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="I234980307a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45">https://www.irb-cisr.gc.ca/en/legal-policy/legal-concepts/Documents/RoaAmr10_e.pdf</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para></list.item></list></para></section.body></section>
10:12: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.f.iii Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Removal orders—Stay of execution</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:12</designator><name date.updated="0">Stay of Removal Order<sep/>Monitoring Compliance with the Conditions of a Stay of Removal</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Pursuant to s. 68(3) of the <ital>IRPA</ital>, where the IAD has stayed a removal order, it may, at any time, on application or on its own initiative, reconsider the appeal. Section 78(1) of the <ital>IAD Rules</ital> allows the Minister or the appellant to make an application to the IAD to reconsider the appeal. Such applications must abide by the requirements set out in s. 85 of the <ital>IAD Rules</ital>, which provides:</para.text><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.section date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124" date.revised="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">85</designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="yeswithspace" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(1)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>Unless these Rules provide otherwise, an application must be made in writing without delay.</bold></stat.text></stat.subsect><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(2)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>In the application, the party must</bold></stat.text><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(a)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>state what decision the party wants the Division to make;</bold></stat.text></stat.para><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(b)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>give reasons why the Division should make that decision; and</bold></stat.text></stat.para><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(c)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>if the views of the other party are known, state whether the other party agrees to the application.</bold></stat.text></stat.para></stat.subsect><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(3)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>Unless these Rules provide otherwise, any evidence that the party wants the Division to consider with a written application must be given in an affidavit or statutory declaration that accompanies the application.</bold></stat.text></stat.subsect><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(4)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>A party who makes a written application must provide</bold></stat.text><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(a)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>to the other party, the application and any accompanying affidavit or statutory declaration; and</bold></stat.text></stat.para><stat.para sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(b)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>to the Division, the application and any accompanying affidavit or statutory declaration, together with a written statement indicating how and when the party provided the documents to the other party.</bold></stat.text></stat.para></stat.subsect><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(5)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>The Division may allow a party to make an application orally at a proceeding if the party demonstrates that, with reasonable effort, they could not have made a written application before the beginning of the proceeding</bold></stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.section></stat.structure></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">When the IAD provides notice that it may reconsider an appeal on its own initiative in which it stayed a removal order, 79(2) of the <ital>IAD Rules</ital> requires that both parties provide the IAD with a written statement concerning compliance with the conditions of the stay of removal within a time specified.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Where a removal order on the grounds of criminal inadmissibility has been stayed, verification of compliance with the conditions imposed by the IAD is the CBSA's responsibility. When a date is scheduled by the IAD for a review, a report indicating compliance, or default, with the conditions shall be prepared with a recommendation to the IAD. Such a recommendation may be to:</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">1</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">allow the appeal, cancel the stay and quash the removal order;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">2</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">maintain the stay for an extended period of time with additional conditions, or removal of conditions which have been met; or</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">3</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">dismiss the appeal and order removal of the appellant as soon as it is possible. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20210811" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Government of Canada, “ENF 19 – Appeals before the Immigration Appeal Division (IAD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB)”, 20 January 2020, online: <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="I234a91a07a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45">https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/ircc/migration/ircc/english/resources/manuals/enf/enf19-eng.pdf</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para></list.item></list></para></section.body></section>
10:13: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.f.iii Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Removal orders—Stay of execution</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:13</designator><name date.updated="0">Stay of Removal Order<sep/>Cancellation of a Stay by Operation of Law</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">A stay is cancelled by operation of law in the circumstances described in s. 68(4) of the <ital>IRPA</ital>. Specifically, if the IAD has stayed a removal order against a permanent resident or a foreign national who was found inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality or criminality, and they are convicted of another offence referred to in subsection 36(1), the stay is cancelled by operation of law and the appeal is terminated.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:14: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i.C Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division—Procedure</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:14</designator><name date.updated="0">Dismiss the appeal</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">If the appeal is dismissed, the removal order becomes enforceable and the CBSA may remove the person from Canada. The person may contest the IAD's decision by asking the Federal Court of Canada permission to apply (i.e., seek leave) for judicial review.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:15: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124" toc.include="y"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:15</designator><name date.updated="0">Early Resolution and Alternative Dispute Resolution</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Lengthy processing times are a major source of frustration and anxiety for those involved in the Canadian appeal process. For appellants separated from their family members, these timelines can be especially distressing. While during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, and as a result of backlogs associated with temporary service disruptions and office closures, it was taking as long as two years to schedule appeal hearings, the shift to hearings via videoconference as the default hearing mode has shown some recent improvement in timelines, especially with the changes in procedure resulting from the new <ital>IAD Rules</ital>. However, the appeals process can still be lengthy.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">To this end, the early resolution process at the IAD aims to streamline appeal processing by identifying certain cases which have the potential to be resolved without the need for a full IAD hearing. The new <ital>IAD Rules</ital>, which requires the Minister's Counsel to provide the appeal record within a shorter time frame, and the appellant to provide disclosure of evidence much earlier in the process, has made it possible for the parties in an appeal to explore the possibility of early resolution much quicker. This new procedure and shortened timeline for disclosure also makes it possible for the parties to identify, much earlier in the appeal process, the relevant issues which can assist should a hearing ultimately be required. At times, an appellant will be asked to provide written submissions in support of the appeal (called a “paper hearing process”). The Hearings Officer representing the CBSA will be given the opportunity to respond and ultimately render an opinion on whether early resolution is appropriate.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">It can be very frustrating when the Hearings Officer's response to a comprehensive package of legal submissions and evidence is a one-line statement that the case is “not suitable” for early resolution and that a full hearing is required. That said, if the Hearings Officer does consent to allowing the appeal through early resolution, then this is an efficient and effective way to resolve the matter, which certainly benefits all parties.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Appellants can also be streamed to attend an Alternative Dispute Resolution (“ADR”) conference, which is an informal hearing involving the appellant and his/her counsel, a Hearings Officer (again, representing the CBSA), and an Early Resolution Officer. As a result of the new <ital>IAD Rules</ital>, the appellant would have submitted a package of evidence and submissions before the ADR conference, and the Hearings Officer will question the appellant at the conference to see if the issues can be resolved without a full hearing. <footnote date.trace="20231124" date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="20231124">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">For further information, see ss. 69-71 of the <ital>IAD Rules</ital>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> This process is less formal than an IAD hearing, as there is usually no Member present to render a decision (rather, it is the parties who are attempting to resolve the matter with the help of the Early Resolution Officer), and the hearing is not recorded. ADR Conferences are generally scheduled for one hour.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">2</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">See the following link for more information about ADR conferences: Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, “Attending an alternative dispute resolution conference at the Immigration Appeal Division”, 24 March 2023, online: <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="I234b54f07a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45">https://irb.gc.ca/en/making-immigration-appeal/Pages/attending-adr-conference.aspx#toc5</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> It is important to note that any information about a matter discussed during an ADR conference is, by default, confidential and cannot be used later in the appeal process unless the information can be obtained in another way unrelated to the ADR conference, it relates to an offence under the <ital>IRPA</ital> or breach of the <ital>IAD Rules</ital>, or the person who gave the information agrees to its disclosure.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">3</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">See s. 66 of the <ital>IAD Rules</ital>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Again, while an ADR conference can be a valuable tool, it is very important to consider the likely outcome. For example, in a spousal sponsorship refusal, the concerns may stem from the intentions of the applicant spouse overseas who is being sponsored. In these types of cases, regardless of how well prepared the sponsoring appellant is, or how strong the evidence and submissions are, the Hearings Officer may still decide that they simply need to hear from the applicant spouse to overcome the credibility concerns - meaning that a full IAD hearing will be required. This can be very disappointing for an appellant who has done everything possible to try to make the ADR process work. Also, if ADR is not successful and a full IAD hearing is required, then this can cause longer delays, as the appellant will be put at the back of the queue for regular IAD scheduling. In most cases, only the appellant is invited to attend the ADR conference and no other witnesses, including applicants (i.e., sponsored family members) are permitted to attend. However, the IAD has indicated that in certain circumstances, applicants may be asked to participate in the ADR conference to answer questions. This is an interesting and important development, as again it can serve, potentially, to greatly shorten the appeal process.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">While it is certainly not the usual course of action to recommend that an appellant opt out of any process which could resolve their appeal, in certain clear cases it may be advisable to wait for a full IAD hearing. On the other hand, for other appellants it may be beneficial to proactively apply for early resolution, depending on the full circumstances of the case and the nature of the refusal.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:16: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:16</designator><name date.updated="0">Serious Criminality</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <ital>Faster Removal of Foreign Criminals Act</ital> (<ital>FRFCA</ital>), <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">S.C. 2013, c. 16.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> which received Royal Assent on 19 June 2013, made a number of changes to the <ital>IRPA</ital>. Most importantly for the discussion herein, s. 24 of the <ital>FRFCA</ital> modified the definition of serious criminality in s. 64(2) of the <ital>IRPA</ital> from a crime punished in Canada by a term of imprisonment of at least two years to a crime punished in Canada by a term of imprisonment of at least six months. This effectively eliminates the right of appeal for those deemed criminally inadmissible who have served a six month sentence or more in Canada. Section 64(1) — (2) of the <ital>IRPA</ital> now reads:</para.text><stat.structure date.updated="0"><stat.section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">64</designator><name date.updated="0">No appeal for inadmissibility</name></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(1)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>No appeal may be made to the Immigration Appeal Division by a foreign national or their sponsor or by a permanent resident if the foreign national or permanent resident has been found to be inadmissible on grounds of security, violating human or international rights, serious criminality or organized criminality.</bold></stat.text></stat.subsect><stat.subsect sameline="no" date.updated="0"><stat.name.block date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>(2)</bold></designator></name.block></stat.name.block><stat.text date.updated="0"><bold>Serious criminality—For the purpose of subsection (1), serious criminality must be with respect to a crime that was punished in Canada by a term of imprisonment of at least six months or that is described in paragraph 36(1)(b) or (c).</bold></stat.text></stat.subsect></stat.section></stat.structure></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">These changes are significant and represent a serious constraint on a permanent resident's access to appeal based on the sentence received. It is thus paramount that immigration counsel are diligent in assisting their clients even <ital>before</ital> they have been convicted and/or sentenced by the criminal courts. This includes contacting criminal counsel as soon as possible. Steps that should then be taken in conjunction with criminal counsel include:</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">1</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Where immigration counsel is able to speak with criminal counsel prior to sentencing, the former should communicate the importance of negotiating with the Crown, where possible, an amendment of the information to a summary offence under the <ital>Criminal Code</ital> rather than a hybrid offence, which is deemed indictable under the <ital>IRPA</ital>. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">2</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124"><ital>IRPA</ital>, S.C. 2001, c. 27 at par. 36(3)(a).</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">2</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Ensure that criminal counsel notes the potential immigration consequences to the client and addresses how these consequences will affect the proportionality of the sentence. Crown counsel and criminal courts can and do often consider the immigration consequences when sentencing, and often a legal opinion from an immigration lawyer as to the immigration consequences of a given sentence is helpful.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">3</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The incorporation of pre-trial custody as credit towards the “term of imprisonment” in the final criminal sentence may have serious negative effects on the right of appeal. Ensure that criminal counsel specifically seek not to have any pre-trial credits on the record, even if time spent in pre-trial custody is counted towards the overall sentence.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">4</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Criminal courts have been willing to consider sentence recalculations for permanent residents who have lost their right of appeal pursuant to ss. 64(1) and (2) of the <ital>IRPA</ital>. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">3</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.trace="20210811" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="R." p2="Pham" post.rptr="15" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="Ibfbd5fd0eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" title="R. v. Pham">R. v. Pham, 2013 SCC 15</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> Therefore, before accepting your client's criminality, it is important to double-check with criminal counsel to explore options that may be available to undo the effects of a criminal sentence; doing so may reposition your client and significantly increase his/her chances of remaining in Canada.</para.text></para></list.item></list></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Immigration lawyers representing clients with criminality can find themselves immersed in a niche world; however, diligent immigration practitioners, when representing clients with criminal records, should always make best efforts to import criminal law evidence and its protections to the immigration context, where possible. Doing so can drastically reposition one's client, even though criminal law evidentiary standards are not always transferable to immigration (administrative) law principles. To take one example, if criminal counsel has argued vehemently for an agreed statement of fact on a conviction (plea, sentencing or otherwise), do not allow that work to be undone by not objecting to the use of one-sided, unproven allegations found in documents such as arrest records and occurrence reports before immigration officers and tribunals. In short, understanding how criminal law is applied and shaping that intersection with immigration principles is the chief responsibility of immigration counsel in advocating for our clients. <ital>For relevant case law on sentencing and rights of appeal, please refer to Appendix “B”.</ital> For further discussion on how the <ital>FRFCA</ital> has affected the determination of the period of inadmissibility applied to a person deemed inadmissible for misrepresentation and subject to a removal order, please see the “Emerging Trends” section of this chapter.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:17: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:17</designator><name date.updated="0">Introduction</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">As noted above, the IAD has an equitable jurisdiction which allows it to consider factors that may warrant an appeal being allowed despite the fact that the decision to issue a removal order is valid in law. Under the <ital>IRPA</ital>, the test of equity which the IAD is to apply has been consolidated into one test for all types of appeals to the IAD by a party other than the Minister. Section 67(1)(c) of the <ital>IRPA</ital> states that the IAD must be satisfied that, at the time the appeal is disposed of, “[…] taking into account the best interests of a child directly affected by the decision, sufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations warrant special relief in light of all the circumstances of the case.”</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In the case of <ital>Ribic v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration)</ital>, <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ribic" p2="Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration)" post.rptr="1357" pre.rptr="1986" ref.id="I94ba15209b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Ribic v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration)">Ribic v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration) (1986), 1986 CarswellNat 1357, [1985] I.A.D.D. No. 4 (Imm. App. Bd.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> the IAD set out a list of six factors that are to be considered in a removal order appeal. The Supreme Court of Canada in <ital>Chieu v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)</ital> reaffirmed that “the factors set out in <ital>Ribic</ital> remain the proper ones for the IAD to consider during an appeal. …” <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">2</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ribic" p2="Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration)" post.rptr="84" pre.rptr="[2002] 1" ref.id="I94ba15219b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Ribic v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration)">Ribic v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration), [2002] 1 S.C.R. 84 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite> at para. 90. The Federal Court of Appeal has considered the extent of the IAD's obligation to exercise its discretion in applying the <ital>Ribic</ital> factors. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ivanov" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)" post.rptr="315" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I94ba3c309b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Ivanov v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)">Ivanov v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2007 FCA 315 (F.C.A.)</ref></cite>, the IAD had cancelled the stay of removal and dismissed the appeal because the appellant had breached the conditions of his stay. Upon judicial review, the Federal Court held that the IAD failed to properly consider three of the relevant <ital>Ribic</ital> factors, namely the potential foreign hardship that the applicant may endure if removed to his country of nationality, the family in Canada and the dislocation to the family that deportation would cause, and the degree of establishment in Canada. Accordingly, the decision was set aside. The Minister appealed the decision to the Court of Appeal. The issue was whether the IAD was supposed to refer to factors not raised in submissions by the appellant in the proceedings before it. The Court of Appeal concluded that once there is evidence that relates to a <ital>Ribic</ital> factor, the IAD must consider that <ital>Ribic</ital> factor in its reasons even if there are not submissions on the point from the appellant. There was no obligation to elicit evidence on the various <ital>Ribic</ital> factors, but an obligation to consider those factors where there was evidence on the point. In <ital>Ivanov</ital>, there was evidence of hardship if removed to the foreign country and as such the IAD had the duty to consider the evidence in relationship to the appropriate <ital>Ribic</ital> factor. The failure constituted an error of law. Therefore, the Minister's appeal was dismissed.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> The <ital>Ribic</ital> factors, including a brief analysis, follow.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:18: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i.D Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division—Evidence</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:18</designator><name date.updated="0">Seriousness of the Offence Leading to the Removal Order (where applicable)</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Some questions that may be considered in determining the seriousness of the offence or offences leading to the removal order are:</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Are they of an organized and repetitive nature or are they motivated by an isolated event/temporary lapse?</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Are they of a violent or a sexual nature?</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Are the crimes generally motivated towards material gain?</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Was the victim of the crime a particularly vulnerable person or group?</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">How severe was the impact on the victim?</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Was the person concerned intoxicated at the time of the offence?</para.text></para></list.item></list></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The appellant should be aware that the IAD Member may rely on the police synopsis of the incidents leading to their conviction in assessing seriousness of the event. The appellant and counsel must be clear that, the fact that a guilty plea was entered does not necessarily confirm the version of events given by police. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">This was confirmed in the case of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Rajagopal" p2="Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness)" post.rptr="523" pre.rptr="2007" ref.id="I94ba3c319b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Rajagopal v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness)">Rajagopal v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness), 2007 FC 523 (F.C.)</ref></cite>. In that case, the appellant was convicted of sexual assault, which resulted in a deportation order on the grounds of serious criminality under para. 36(1)(a) of the <ital>IRPA.</ital> After applying the <ital>Ribic</ital> factors, the IAD dismissed his appeal. During the appeal hearing, the appellant provided testimony as to his version of the events leading up to the sexual assault charges, a version that was materially different from the police occurrence report that was also filed into evidence. In its decision, the IAD noted that because: “the appellant pled guilty to the charge as described in the report, I find that I prefer the above over the testimony of the appellant and that it is the truth as to what happened, on a balance of probabilities.” On judicial review of the IAD decision, Justice Mosley concluded that the IAD's reliance on the applicant's guilty plea as a verification of the police report was unreasonable. The Court noted it would have been open to the IAD to find that the police synopsis was the more reliable version of events, it is inappropriate for it to have been assumed. Though the IAD could have referred to evidence or testimony to support an argument that on a balance of probabilities the police report likely characterized the underlying facts of the offence in an accurate manner, the IAD did not do so, and thus committed a reviewable error. The <ital>Rajagopal</ital> decision remains the leading decision on this issue.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:19: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i.D Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division—Evidence</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:19</designator><name date.updated="0">Possibility of Rehabilitation (where applicable)</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Federal Court had an opportunity to review the standard of proof that is to be applied by the IAD in assessing the <bold> <underscore>possibility</underscore></bold> of an appellant's rehabilitation. In the case of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Martinez-Soto" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)" post.rptr="883" pre.rptr="2008" ref.id="I94ba63409b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Martinez-Soto v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)">Martinez-Soto v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2008 FC 883 (F.C.)</ref></cite>, the applicant was found to be a Convention refugee in 1986. He had struggled with alcohol addiction for some time, owing largely to anxiety he experienced because of the trauma of witnessing El Salvadoran death squads in action. His alcohol abuse contributed to a lengthy history of criminality, which culminated in a conviction for assault causing bodily harm. After this conviction, the applicant quit alcohol, became compliant with court-ordered supervision and he began to show signs of improvement. Nevertheless, he was found inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality and, as a consequence, he sought a stay of his deportation from the IAD. The IAD denied his appeal because it determined he had not proved, on the civil balance of probabilities, that he had rehabilitated himself. On judicial review, the Court found that the IAD had erred in its application of the assessment of the applicant's rehabilitation. Pursuant to the <ital>Ribic</ital> factors, the Court found that the Board was obligated to consider the possibility of rehabilitation, rather than proof of rehabilitation already accomplished. It was clarified in <ital>Ramirez</ital> <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>Ramirez Martinez, Jose Mauricio (aka Jose Mauricio Ramirez) v. M.E.I.</ital>, IAD T95-065669 at para. 3.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> that to demonstrate the potential for rehabilitation, appellant's must provide “credible expressions of remorse, articulation of genuine understanding as to the nature and consequences of criminal behaviour, and demonstrable efforts to address the factors that give rise to such behaviour”. For this final point, professional reports are often essential. This may include reports from probation officers, doctors, mental health care professionals and/or addiction counsellors.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:20: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i.D Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division—Evidence</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:20</designator><name date.updated="0">Length of Time Spent in Canada and the Degree of Establishment</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Under this prong of the test, the Board will consider a number of factors to determine the appellant's degree of establishment in Canada. This typically includes an analysis of the appellant's employment and academic history, his or her assets in Canada, any memberships or involvement in local organizations, as well as the appellant's family relations in Canada. The amount of time spent in Canada that will weigh in the appellant's favour will vary depending on the specific facts of a case. An appellant may have been living in Canada for most of his or her life, but if the appellant has a serious conviction or minimal establishment, the long-term residence may not go far in offsetting the other concerns. In addition, little weight will be assigned to the appellant's establishment if it occurred through fraudulent conduct. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>Lin v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)</ital> (October 2, 2014), Doc. 5239-0138, T83-01023 (Can. I.R.B.) at para. 20.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:21: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i.D Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division—Evidence</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:21</designator><name date.updated="0">Family in Canada and the Dislocation Caused by Removal</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">The existence of large numbers of an appellant's immediate family members in Canada is generally a strong humanitarian and compassionate factor in their favour. In cases where an appellant makes a significant financial contribution to their household, the impact of dislocation to the family in Canada is a factor that should be stressed by the appellant. Similarly, if the appellant is actively involved in providing care to any Canadian children, this should be stressed to the Board. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Dennis" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)" post.rptr="196" pre.rptr="2004" ref.id="I94ba63419b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Dennis v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)">Dennis v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2004 FC 196 (F.C.)</ref></cite>, the Court considered a ss. 64(2) removal order in light of Article 7(1) of the United Nation's Convention on the Rights of the Child. The Court held, applying <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Martinez" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)" post.rptr="1341" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I94ba63429b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Martinez v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)">Martinez v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2003 FC 1341 (F.C.)</ref></cite> that, in spite of the serious criminality of the individual, regard must be had for the children of the father who was about to be deported. However, the Court has also found that there need not be specific reference to a parent's role as financial provider in order to demonstrate that the IAD has considered this factor in determining the best interests of the children within the removal context. In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cai" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)" post.rptr="748" pre.rptr="2016" ref.id="I94ba8a509b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Cai v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)">Cai v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 748 (F.C.)</ref></cite>, the Court considered the reasonableness of an exclusion order issued as a result of a misrepresentation; the Applicant's status in Canada had been achieved by way of a marriage-of-convenience. The Applicant was the owner of a successful seafood business. His wife, who came to Canada as an immigrant investor investing $2.0 million, was not working at the time of the removal, making the Applicant the sole financial support for the family. The Court found that, despite not explicitly addressing the Applicant's role as financial provider and caregiver, the IAD had been satisfied on the evidence that the Applicant fulfilled the normal role of a father to young children. The Court noted that based on the record, there was no suggestion that the family would not be able to support itself, even if the applicant were forced to close his business as a result of his removal.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> Evidence should be submitted to demonstrate the existence of a close family and the fact that the appellant's deportation would be a psychological, emotional, and/or financial hardship for the appellant's family members in Canada.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:22: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i.D Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division—Evidence</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:22</designator><name date.updated="0">Family and Community Support</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Under this prong of the test, it is necessary for the appellant to submit evidence to demonstrate that he or she has a strong support network in Canada. In particular, an appellant should be able to demonstrate that they have family, friends, and/or community members who will ensure that they have a stable living environment, that the appellant obtains whatever treatment or counselling may be necessary, and that the appellant does not get involved in any further criminal activity.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">It is especially important that friends, family and/or community members appear at the hearing to provide oral testimony before the IAD. The panel is likely to make a negative inference if no friends or family members appear to testify in support of the appellant.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:23: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i.D Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division—Evidence</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block date.trace="20210811" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:23</designator><name date.updated="0">Hardship of Return to Country of Nationality</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Although a full risk assessment is generally reserved for the Pre-Removal Risk Assessment stage of the removal process, the IAD nonetheless has an obligation to consider the appellant's hardship that the appellant may face should they be removed and return to their country of nationality. Under this prong of the test the IAD may consider:</para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Whether the appellant has family or any other support network in the country of return that would be able to provide assistance in their resettlement;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Whether the appellant has any medical conditions, and if so, whether any treatment is available in the country of return;</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">General conditions in the country of return; and</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Any exceptional hardship that would result from the appellant being uprooted from Canada. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">It is important to note that in <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Suresh" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)" post.rptr="1" pre.rptr="2002" ref.id="I94ba8a519b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Suresh v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)">Suresh v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2002 SCC 1 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, the Supreme Court of Canada held that the removal of an individual to a country where there was a serious risk of torture would in all but the most exceptional circumstances violate the principles of fundamental justice protected by s. 7 of the <ital>Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms</ital>. Thus, where an appellant can establish that his or her risk upon return is severe, this is a factor that should weigh heavily against the appellant's removal from Canada. In a case where risk of return has been established, a panel must engage in a “fundamental justice balance”, by addressing the extent to which the exercise of its discretion is affected by s. 7 <ital>Charter</ital> rights, and the implications of <ital>Suresh</ital>, in order to determine whether the execution of the removal order would violate the principles of fundamental justice.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para></list.item></list></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">It has been established by the Federal Court of Appeal that Convention refugees and protected persons are not subject to this step of the <ital>Ribic</ital> analysis, as the principle of non-refoulement <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">2</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>IRPA</ital>, at s. 115.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> prevents such appellants from being returned to their country of nationality. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">3</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Balathavarajan" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)" post.rptr="340" pre.rptr="2006" ref.id="I94bab1609b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Balathavarajan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)">Balathavarajan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2006 FCA 340 (F.C.A.)</ref></cite>, the applicant, a Convention refugee, was convicted of several crimes and was issued a deportation order. The applicant appealed the order to the Immigration Appeal Division on the basis that humanitarian and compassionate considerations warranted special relief in light of all the circumstances of the case. The IAD considered five of the six <ital>Ribic</ital> factors in determining whether special relief was warranted. However, the IAD refused to consider the last factor, namely, the hardship of return to the country of removal, as it found (given the applicant's refugee status) that Sri Lanka was not a “likely country of removal” for the purposes of s. 115 of the <ital>IRPA</ital>. The IAD denied the appeal. At the Federal Court, the applications judge upheld the decision of the IAD, but certified the following question: Is a Deportation Order, with respect to a permanent resident who has been declared to be a convention refugee, which specifies as sole country of citizenship the country which he fled as a refugee, sufficient without more to establish that country as the likely country of removal so that <ital>Chieu</ital> applies and the IAD is required to consider hardship to the Applicant in that country on an appeal from a Deportation Order? The Court of Appeal upheld the IAD's decision. It concluded that the applicant could not (absent a danger opinion) be refouled to that country and therefore it was unnecessary to consider the effect that removal to Sri Lanka would have on the applicant. Furthermore, given that there was no other likely country of removal, the Court concluded that the IAD was under no obligation to consider the potential for foreign hardship in determining whether to grant special relief. Last, it is has been held that an appellant must exhaust his/her appeal rights at the IAD prior to proceeding to Federal Court. Also, an appellant cannot be limited in his/her submissions before the IAD by a panel member.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para></section.body></section>
