10:24IntroductionSection 36 of the IRPA establishes two types of inadmissibility:•serious criminality, in the case of foreign nationals and permanent residents; and•criminality in the case of a foreign national.Inadmissibility for criminality or serious criminality results from three types of acts, namely:1a conviction in Canada;2a conviction outside Canada equivalent to a criminal offence in Canada;3an act outside Canada that would constitute a criminal offence in Canada.A fourth act, which applies only to criminality, can give rise to inadmissibility where a foreign national committed an act that is an offence under an Act of Parliament (i.e., Federal law) prescribed by regulations upon entering Canada.It is under the classes of offences committed outside of Canada (for which a conviction may or may not have been registered) that an equivalency analysis becomes necessary. “Equivalency” can be determined in three ways: 1Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada. “ENF 1 – Inadmissibility”, pp. 39-40, online: https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/ircc/migration/ircc/english/resources/manuals/enf/enf01-eng.pdf.•by comparison of the precise wording in each statute both through documents and, if available, through the evidence of an expert or experts in the law of the foreign jurisdiction with a view to determining the essential elements of the respective offences;•by examining the evidence adduced before the member of the Immigration Division, both oral and documentary, to ascertain whether or not that evidence was sufficient to establish that the essential elements of the offence in Canada had been proven in the foreign proceedings, whether precisely described in the initiating documents or in the statutory provisions in the same words or not; or•by a combination of the two2This guidance follows from the decision Hill v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration) (1987), 73 N.R. 315 (Fed. C.A.), as confirmed in Pardhan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2007 FC 756, paras. 10-11. Pardhan has remained the leading case in determining criminal equivalency, and continues to be followed by the Federal Court. See Singh v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 946 (F.C.) at paras. 16-17, and Cruz v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 455 (F.C.) at paras. 42-43.The IRCC Policy Manual 3Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, “ENF 1 – Inadmissibility”, pp. 39-40, online: Government of Canada https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/ircc/migration/ircc/english/resources/manuals/enf/enf01-eng.pdf. (“Manual”) provides the following guidance to hearings officers preparing an admissibility case where equivalency of a foreign offence must be established:When preparing a case that involves an offence in a foreign jurisdiction that may be equivalent to an offence in Canada, hearings officers should follow these steps:Step 1Identify the foreign offence.Step 2Obtain evidence on the foreign offence. You should address the following three areas:  • the wording of the offence in the foreign statute;  • the best proof of a conviction (see ENF1 Section 7 for acceptable types of evidence);  • details of what was actually done (the act).Step 3Identify possible Canadian equivalent offence(s)Step 4Break down each offence (Canadian and foreign) into its basic elements (see ENF2 Section 3/7 and ENF2 Appendix A)Step 5Compare each foreign element to its Canadian equivalent and determine if the Canadian element is equal to, broader than or narrower than the foreign element.Step 6When the Canadian element is narrower than the foreign element, you will be required to examine the act (the details of the offence) to determine whether the act committed satisfies the Canadian element.Step 7Come to an overall conclusion as to whether the foreign offence is equivalent to the Canadian offence by finding that the foreign elements are equal to or narrower [than] the Canadian element and where broader than the act in question meets the Canadian element.Step 8If you have equivalency, take into account the penalty for the Canadian offence at the time the offence was committed to decide which allegation under A36 is appropriate.
The foreign law must be proven during the admissibility hearing by producing all the extracts relevant to the offence, which will be entered as an exhibit. The relevant extracts should, as a rule, include the sections that define the terms used in describing the offence.As seen above, in the examination of equivalency, a determination is made as to whether each of the essential elements of the foreign offence is present in the Canadian equivalent. The following are helpful ways to remember when you have equivalency:•If all the elements exist in both statutes (Canadian and foreign), the offences are equivalent. It is not necessary for the wording of the two laws to be identical. For example, the term “knowingly” may be equivalent to “knowing”, and the term “whoever” may be equivalent to “any person”.•If the foreign enactment is more restrictive than the Canadian enactment, both offences are equivalent, since the Canadian statute covers all the situations contemplated in the foreign statute.•If the foreign enactment is broader than the Canadian statute, or if the text includes situations that do not lead to a criminal offence in Canada, there is no textual equivalency. However the analysis does not end there. It is then necessary to examine the circumstances of the offence to determine if there is equivalency nonetheless. When this situation arises, evidence should be submitted regarding the facts that were proven in the criminal trial held outside Canada or, in cases where there is no conviction, evidence such as police reports may be relied upon to show that an offence was committed. When every essential element of the Canadian offence can be established, there is equivalence.•The hearings officer should identify for the benefit of the ID which constituting element(s) of the Canadian offence is (are) not found in the text of the foreign offence. The hearings officer should then identify the facts that establish each element in the Canadian offence by referring to exhibits or part of a testimony that prove these facts.4Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, “ENF 3 – Admissibility Hearings and Detention Reviews”, pg. 34-35, online: https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/ircc/migration/ircc/english/resources/manuals/enf/enf-3-admissibility-(en)-final.pdf.The Manual sets out the following example, which is helpful in understanding how an analysis is conducted when the Canadian offence is more restrictive than the foreign offence:General Laws of Massachusetts, Pt IV, Title I, Ch. 266, sec. 49 – Burglarious instruments; making; possession; useWhoever makes or mends, or begins to make or mend, or knowingly has in his possession, an engine, machine, tool or implement adapted and designed for cutting through, forcing or breaking open a building, room, vault, safe or other depository, in order to steal therefrom money or other property, or to commit any other crime, knowing the same to be adapted and designed for the purpose aforesaid, with intent to use or employ or allow the same to be used or employed for such purpose, or whoever knowingly has in his possession a master key designed to fit more than one motor vehicle, with intent to use or employ the same to steal a motor vehicle or other property therefrom […]Criminal Code of Canada, sec 351(1) – Possession of break-in instruments351 (1) Every person who, without lawful excuse, has in their possession any instrument suitable for the purpose of breaking into any place, motor vehicle, vault or safe knowing that the instrument has been used or is intended to be used for that purpose,Comparing the text of these two provisions we see that there is no textual equivalency. The Canadian offence is more restrictive since the instruments described under the Canadian offence do not address the act of making or mending the break-in instruments.To equate with the Canadian criminal code definition of breaking in, it is necessary to introduce evidence showing that person was found in possession of the instrument that was in working order to commit the offence and was not arrested while in the process of making said break-in instrument.In this example, the evidence that the foreign offence is equivalent to an offence committed in Canada could consist of the following:•introduction of the relevant sections of the foreign statute; and•testimony of the person concerned describing the circumstances of their arrest and type of instrument; or•extracts of the transcript of the foreign trial identifying the nature of the instruments; or•copy of the foreign indictment which contains a description of the instruments found; or•documentary evidence providing a description of the instruments.In most admissibility hearings dealing with equivalency, the hearings office will generally have to produce the following documents as exhibits, when available:•evidence of the conviction, such as a certificate of conviction, a police report or a statutory declaration outlining a telephone conversation with a police officer, court reporter, court records clerk, or any document originating from the authorities of the country where the conviction was handed down;•the legal description of the foreign offence; that is, the text of the statutory provision under which the person was convicted; and•evidence (obtained from the charge or indictment or a similar document) of the particulars of the offence [Brannson v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (para. 4)]. In some cases, the certificate of conviction may contain sufficient information for the certificate to be used instead of the indictment.5Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, “ENF 3 – Admissibility Hearings and Detention Reviews”, pg. 35-36, online: https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/ircc/migration/ircc/english/resources/manuals/enf/enf-3-admissibility-(en)-final.pdf.

The first is a simple analysis of facts providing a comparison of foreign legislation to Canadian statutes. The second provides an example of submissions made in support of an individual facing removal as a result of their foreign criminality.Sample Case #1A 44(1) report is written against the foreign national or permanent resident alleging:1Person concerned is involved in criminal activity in Hong Kong that resulted in obtaining HK $2.2 million by altering terms and conditions of insurance policies without company's or client's knowledge;2The theft of monies was discovered when clients requested their policies from the company;3Actions if taken in Canada would have led to conviction for indictable offences under ss. 334 (for a s. 322 offence) and 362(1) of the Canadian Criminal Code for which terms of imprisonment not exceeding 10 years might be imposed;4The acts of the person concerned are alleged to be contrary to s. 19(1)(a) of the Theft Ordinance, Cap. 210, Laws of Hong Kong — totalling 19 counts of false accounting.Equivalency Analysis1Canada's Criminal Code sections mentioned in the s. 44(1) report are not equivalent to the Hong Kong offence.2According to the case law, the defences for both the relevant Hong Kong and Canadian offences must be considered when doing equivalency analysis. 1Li v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration, [1997] 1 F.C. 235 (Fed. C.A.). The relevant version of the Criminal Code for the purposes of the equivalency analysis is the version in force at the time of the adjudication. 2Ward v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 1996 CarswellNat 2286 (Fed. T.D.). The Court noted that evidence wasn't sufficient to establish that the essential ingredients of the offence in Canada had been proved in the foreign jurisdiction according to the version of the Criminal Code at time of the inquiry. Confirmed more recently in Tran v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2017 SCC 50 (S.C.C.), paras. 35, 38, 53. Please note that IRCC has recently clarified that where “the maximum punishment for the offence under Canadian law has become more lenient between the time of the commission of the offence and the time of the inadmissibility determination, officers are advised to apply the spirit of the Charter, which accords the benefit of the more lenient penalty. Therefore, officers should look at the maximum possible punishment under Canadian law at the time of the inadmissibility assessment.”3Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, “Assessing inadmissibility due to serious criminality following Tran v. This would also be in accordance with the Supreme Court of Canada findings in Tran v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2017 SCC 50 (S.C.C.).3There can be no switching between the criminality provisions as set out in the s. 44 report.4It is established that where the foreign offence is narrower than the Canadian offence, a finding of equivalence can be made unless there are relevant defences available with respect to the offence in Canada, which are not available in the foreign jurisdiction. In contrast, where the foreign jurisdiction is broader than the Canadian offence, all the elements of the Canadian offence must be contained in the acts committed by the person.5The case law calls for a word-for-word comparison of the Hong Kong provisions as against ss. 322, and 362 of the Criminal Code. For reference, these provisions read as follows:Section 19(1)(a) of the Theft Ordinance, Cap. 210, Laws of Hong Kong“where a person dishonestly, with a view to gain for himself or another or with intent to cause loss to another—destroys, defaces, conceals or falsifies any account or any record or document made or required for any accounting purpose; … he shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable on conviction upon indictment to imprisonment for 10 years”Sections 322(1) and 362(1) of the Criminal Code of Canada322 (1) Every one commits theft who fraudulently and without colour of right takes, or fraudulently and without colour of right converts to his use or to the use of another person, anything, whether animate or inanimate, with intent(a) to deprive, temporarily or absolutely, the owner of it, or a person who has a special property or interest in it, of the thing or of his property or interest in it;(b) to pledge it or deposit it as security;(c) to part with it under a condition with respect to its return that the person who parts with it may be unable to perform; or(d) to deal with it in such a manner that it cannot be restored in the condition in which it was at the time it was taken or converted.Subsections (2), (3), (4), and (5) of s. 322 all serve to refine or elaborate upon the general elements of theft found in s. 322(1) as follows:•subsection (2) serves to broaden theft to include moving something or causing something to be moved, in conjunction with the necessary theft intent;•subsection (3) provides that the element of “fraudulently” does not require secrecy or concealment;•subsection (4) elaborates upon the element of “conversion” as not requiring actual possession by the person committing theft; and•subsection (5) deals expressly with the taking of wild living creatures.None of these subsections appear to be 1) essential elements, in a direct sense, of the offence of theft; or 2) relevant to the matter at hand. They are therefore not subject to analysis as against the Hong Kong provision.362 (1) Every one commits an offence who(a) by a false pretence, whether directly or through the medium of a contract obtained by a false pretence, obtains anything in respect of which the offence of theft may be committed or causes it to be delivered to another person;(b) obtains credit by a false pretence or by fraud;(c) knowingly makes or causes to be made, directly or indirectly, a false statement in writing with intent that it should be relied on, with respect to the financial condition or means or ability to pay of himself or herself or any person or organization that he or she is interested in or that he or she acts for, for the purpose of procuring, in any form whatever, whether for his or her benefit or the benefit of that person or organization,(i) the delivery of personal property,(ii) the payment of money,(iii) the making of a loan,(iv) the grant or extension of credit,(v) the discount of an account receivable, or(vi) the making, accepting, discounting or endorsing of a bill of exchange, cheque, draft or promissory note; or(d) knowing that a false statement in writing has been made with respect to the financial condition or means or ability to pay of himself or herself or another person or organization that he or she is interested in or that he or she acts for, procures on the faith of that statement, whether for his or her benefit or for the benefit of that person or organization, anything mentioned in subparagraphs (c)(i) to (vi).6The line by line analysis is as follows:Wording of Hong Kong offenceWording of s. 322 of the Criminal CodeActor: [A person] shall be guilty of an offence Punishment: and shall be liable on conviction upon indictment to imprisonment for 10 years [who]: Adverb: Dishonestly Intent Requirement: with a view to gain for himself or another or with intent to cause loss to another Action: destroys, defaces, conceals or falsifies any account or any record or document made or required for Object of Action: any accounting purpose …Actor: Everyone commits theft who Punishment: [s. 334 of the Code prescribes the punishment for theft in this case] Adverb: Fraudulently and without colour of right Intent Requirement: with intent to deprive, temporarily or absolutely the owner of it Action: takes … or converts to his use or to the use of another Object of Action: anything
Line 1 — ActorThese lines are equivalent.Line 2 — PunishmentIn the Canadian Criminal Code, the punishment provisions relevant to theft as defined by s. 322 will be determined by the value of the item stolen. In this case, the relevant provision is s. 334. Considering s. 334, these lines appear to be equivalent. In any event, there does not seem to be any case law authority for the proposition that the quantum of the punishment is relevant to an equivalency determination.Line 3 — AdverbThese lines are arguably not equivalent.“Dishonestly” is the essential element of the Hong Kong offence.“Fraudulently and without colour of right” is the Canadian counterpart.These terms “Fraudulently and without colour of right” have been considered in detail in Canadian jurisprudence. “Fraudulently”, in Canadian jurisprudence, requires an element of dishonesty. 4R. v. DeMarco (1973), 13 C.C.C. (2d) 369 (Ont. C.A.). However, the Canadian provision also requires that there be a lack of “colour of right”. According to case law, a person acts with colour of right when he or she has a right to take something, or honestly but mistakenly believes that he or she has the colour of right. 5R. v. DeMarco (1973), 13 C.C.C. (2d) 369 (Ont. C.A.). In R. v. DeMarco, the Court held, at paras. 9 and 10, that the existence of a colour of right negates fraud. There may be an absence of any fraudulent intention, however, notwithstanding the absence of a colour of right to do the act in question, for example, with the taking of another's property temporarily by way of prank. This interpretation was more recently confirmed in R. v. Simpson, 2015 SCC 40. The Court in Demarco also held that the conduct is not found to be fraudulent merely because it is unauthorized, unless it is dishonest and morally wrong. In light of this, the Canadian provision is narrower than the Hong Kong counterpart because there is an additional requirement of a lack of colour of right to trigger a conviction under s. 322.Line 4 — Intent RequirementWhile there is some equivalency between these two provisions, there are also differences, including that the Hong Kong section is broader in scope. The Hong Kong provision calls for an intent to 1) gain for himself or another; or 2) cause loss to another. The Canadian provision merely calls for an intent to deprive the owner. A person who demonstrated only an intent to gain for himself — thus satisfying the Hong Kong requirement — would not be liable for conviction under the Canadian section.Line 5 — ActionThese lines are also not equivalent: “destroys, defaces, conceals or falsifies” in the Hong Kong provision cannot be reasonably read to be equivalent to “takes … or converts to his use or to the use of another”.Line 6 — Object of ActionThese lines are not equivalent, though the Canadian provision encompasses the scope of the Hong Kong provision. The Hong Kong section calls for the object of the conduct to be “any account or record”, whereas the Canadian provision refers to “anything” that can be stolen. On a plain reading, the term “anything” encompasses an “account or record”; thus, if the person concerned were convicted of the offence in Hong Kong, the person concerned would be open to a finding of guilt under the broader Canadian provision as well.7In comparing s. 362 of the Criminal Code:Wording of Hong Kong offenceWording of section 362 of the Criminal Code Actor: [A person] shall be guilty of an offence  Punishment: and shall be liable on conviction upon indictment to imprisonment for 10 years [who]:  Adverb: Dishonestly  Intent Requirement: with a view to gain for himself or another or with intent to cause loss to another  Action: destroys, defaces, conceals or falsifies  Object of Action: any account or any record or document made or required for any accounting purpose … Actor: Every one commits an offence who …  Punishment: [Punishment provisions in s. 362(2) of the Criminal Code]  Adverb: by a false pretence*  *Clarification of Adverb: *defined in section 361(1) as: a) a representation of a matter of fact either present or past …  b) Made by words or otherwise  Intention Requirement: with intent that it should be relief on, with respect to the financial condition or mean or ability to pay of himself or herself or any person or organization that he or she is interested in or that he or she acts for.  Action: obtains anything … or causes it to be delivered to another person whether directly or through the medium of a contract obtained by false pretence  Object of Action: [anything] in respect of which the offence of theft may be committed
Line 1 — ActorThese lines are equivalent.Line 2 — PunishmentThese lines appear to be equivalent. In any event, again there is no case law authority for the proposition that the quantum of the punishment is relevant to an equivalency determination.Line 3 — AdverbThese lines are not equivalent. This is the crux of the equivalency analysis in this particular instance. The terms “dishonestly” and “by a false pretence” are the primary essential elements of both the Canadian and Hong Kong offences. However, “false pretence” is expressly defined in the Criminal Code (as described below), and this highlights essential differences between the two provisions.Lines 4, 5, and 6 — Clarification of AdverbThere is no Hong Kong equivalent to the term “false pretences” found in the Canadian provision. The three separate elements of the “false pretences” definition are not captured by the essential elements of the Hong Kong offence.Line 7 — Intent RequirementThese lines are equivalent, based on a plain reading.Line 8 — ActionAgain, these lines are not equivalent. “Destroys, defaces, conceals or falsifies” in the Hong Kong provision cannot be reasonably read to be equivalent to the term “obtains anything…” Note that line 8 of the Hong Kong offence does use the term “falsifies”, which is similar to the Canadian term found in line 6 of the chart. However, these provisions are too dissimilar to be relevant for consideration.Line 9 — Object of ActionThese lines are not equivalent. The Hong Kong provision calls for the object of the conduct to be “any account or record”, whereas the Canadian provision refers to “anything” that can be stolen.8Based upon the aforementioned analysis, the essential elements of the offences would be as follows:In order to sustain a charge of theft under subsection 19(1)(a) of the Theft Ordinance, Cap. 210, Laws of Hong Kong, the following must be established:•the identity of the accused;•that the accused destroyed, defaced, concealed or falsified any account, record or accounting document;•that in doing so, the accused acted dishonestly;•that in doing so, the accused also intended to either effect gain for himself or cause loss to someone else.In the Hong Kong decision of Kin, the Court succinctly set out the relevant test: the court must be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt as to the elements of dishonesty and with a view to gain for another. There must be objective dishonesty by the standards of ordinary people and subjective dishonesty. Did the accused realise that it was dishonest by those standards? In order to sustain a charge of theft under s. 322 of the Criminal Code, the following must be established beyond a reasonable doubt: 6See R. v. Herceg, 1998 CarswellOnt 413, [1998] O.J. No. 434 (Ont. Gen. Div.), at 8, for more information.•the identity of the accused;•that “anything” was taken;•that the property taken belongs to the victim;•that required intent was present, specifically;•the taking was done fraudulently;•the taking was done without colour of right;•the accused intended to deprive the owner of the item when he took it.In order to sustain a charge under s. 362 of the Criminal Code, the following essential elements must be established beyond a reasonable doubt:•the identity of the accused;•that the accused used a “false pretence”;•there was a representation of fact, made by words or otherwise;•the accused knew the representation to be false;•the representation was made with fraudulent intent to induce the person receiving it to act on it;•the accused obtained “anything” because of the false pretence;•that “anything” was something that could be the subject of theft.The primary defences to counteract an allegation of theft appear to be that:•there was an absence of fraudulent intent (e.g., offence committed by way of prank); 7R. v. DeMarco (1973), 13 C.C.C. (2d) 369 (Ont. C.A.).•a colour of right existed (e.g., the accused can assert a proprietary or possessory right to the item taken, or alternatively has an honest but mistaken belief in that right); 8R. v. DeMarco (1973), 13 C.C.C. (2d) 369 (Ont. C.A.).•there is no proof of ownership of the item taken; 9Little v. R. (1974), 19 C.C.C. (2d) 385 (S.C.C.).•there is no proof that the item was capable of being owned/stolen 10R. v. Smith, [1962] S.C.R. 215 (S.C.C.). (e.g., in the case of intangibles);•there is no proof that the item was “taken”;•there is no proof that there was “deprivation” within the meaning of s. 322 of the Criminal Code.The primary defences to counteract an allegation of obtaining something by false pretences appear to be that:•there was no “representation” for the purposes of s. 361(1), which defines “false pretence”;•the representation did not concern a matter of fact;•the representation concerned neither a matter of present fact or past fact (e.g., it was a representation concerning the future);•the accused did not know the representation was false;•the representation was not made with fraudulent intent;•by making the representation, the accused did not obtain “anything” directly or indirectly;•the “anything” that the accused obtained is not capable of being stolen.The primary defences to counteract an allegation of theft pursuant to the Hong provision appear to be that:•there was an absence of fraudulent intent (e.g., no dishonesty); 11R. v. DeMarco (1973), 13 C.C.C. (2d) 369 (Ont. C.A.).•there was no proof of gain for the perpetrator or for another;•there is no proof that the item was “taken”.It is therefore submitted that the Canadian Criminal Code section mentioned in the s. 44(1) Report (s. 362) is not equivalent to the Hong Kong offence. As well, s. 322 of the Code, which is incorporated by reference to s. 334 in the Report, bears some similarities, but overall is likely not an equivalent provision.Sample Case #2Below are sample submissions providing an equivalency analysis. By way of background, the proposed applicant in this matter was refused a permanent residence supported by an application to sponsor (“spousal sponsorship”) as a result of a “caution” that he received in the United Kingdom in 2006 for assault occasioning actual bodily harm. The applicant was cautioned on the same day for offences against the person. The applicant, along with his brother, intervened in what they believed to be a domestic violence assault and quickly found themselves defending against both the perpetrator and the female victim, who was struck in the face (the mouth) by the applicant in the struggle. An entry is made in the Computer Assisted Immigration Processing System (“CAIPS”) alleging:•Whilst PI was cautioned in 2006 rather than convicted by the court;•Under the UK Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974, a caution is not a conviction and there is no rehabilitation period associated with a caution. Under the UK Act, individuals with only a caution on their criminal record can answer no if asked whether they have a criminal record. Therefore, PI is not criminally inadmissible for caution in relation to above charges.•Processing to continue.A senior immigration officer (“SIO”) then conducts the following equivalency analysis, leading to the refusal of the application. The SIO determined:•“Assault Occasioning Actual Bodily Harm.” If committed in Canada, this offence would be punishable under s. 267(b) of the Criminal Code and would be punishable by way of indictment and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years;•In Summary: the applicant has received a caution, which is an admission of guilt for assault occasioning bodily harm in 2006.•This is a serious offence, more than common assault…•Assault for occasioning bodily harm is indictable and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years…this comes within s. 36(1)(c) of the Act. The applicant therefore comes within an inadmissible class of persons.Sample Reply SubmissionRelevant Issues and Law — Section 36(1)(c) of the IRPAWe felt it prudent to discuss the intent behind this provision of the IRPA, as it is especially relevant to this proposed case. The IRCC manuals indicate that as part of Canada's international commitment to combat trans-national crime, the policy intent in applying the provisions is first and foremost “to deny entry into Canada and thereby prevent Canadian territory being used as a safe haven by persons who are subject to a criminal proceeding in a foreign jurisdiction; or are fleeing from such proceedings.” 12Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, “ENF 2 — Evaluating Inadmissibility”. Note: this manual is no longer publicly available.The applicant is not the subject of a warrant, has no charges pending, nor was he ever convicted of any act. Additionally, he is not fleeing prosecution. 13Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, “ENF 2 — Evaluating Inadmissibility”. Note: this manual is no longer publicly available. The “committing an act” provisions of the Act are not intended to bar the entry into Canada of persons who may have committed, but have not been convicted of, one or more summary offences. 14Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, “ENF 2 — Evaluating Inadmissibility”. Note: this manual is no longer publicly available. Rather, it appears that the practical application of the policy with respect to the “committing an act” provisions is to deny entry into Canada to persons against whom there is evidence of criminal activity that could result in a conviction if there were a prosecution in Canada. Kindly refer to the information contained in the “equivalency, findings and defence” sections herein.Policy indicates that the ‘committing an act’ provisions should not be used in the following circumstances:•in most cases, when authorities in the foreign jurisdiction indicate they would not lay a charge or make known to an officer their decision or intent to drop the charges;•the person admits to committing the act but has been pardoned or the record is expunged.We submit that these very circumstances are relevant to the applicant's particular facts and we respectfully request you consider same.It is also equally important to note that it is not the government's intention that the s. 36(1)(c) of the IRPA provision be used as an alternative to prosecution.A CautionKindly consider the following guidance from the UK Sentencing Council in connection with defining a caution, its purpose, when it is relevant and should be utilized, its effect on any future criminality, etc:A simple caution may be issued where there is evidence that the offender has committed an offence, the offender admits to the offence, it is not in the public interest to prosecute and the offender agrees to being given the caution.When sentencing an offender who has received a simple caution on a previous occasion:•the caution is not a previous conviction and, therefore, is not a statutory aggravating factor;•however, the caution will form part of the offender's criminal record and if the caution is recent and is relevant to the current offence it may be considered to be an aggravating factor15Sentencing Council, “Simple Caution”, online: Government of the UK https://www.sentencingcouncil.org.uk/explanatory-material/magistrates-court/item/out-of-court-disposals/3-simple-caution/.By the very virtue of the reference to a “simple caution” it assists the reader in determining the genesis behind same; i.e., a ‘warning’.Further FindingsA caution is not tantamount to, or in any way comparable to, a finding of guilt or conviction to assault occasioning actual bodily harm before a court of law. Consider the decision of Dhadwar v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness), 16Dhadwar v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness), 2008 FC 482 (F.C.). wherein Justice Blanchard found that, while it is open to the board to rely on evidence it finds to be relevant, credible and trustworthy, it should not mischaracterize the nature of such evidence. Citing the decision of Justice Mosley in Rajagopal v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness), 17Rajagopal v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness), 2007 FC 523 (F.C.). Justice Blanchard noted at para. 29, that a police report contained allegations as recorded by the police officer upon investigation of the complaint, not the findings of fact reached by a court. Justice Blanchard stated:As stated above, the police report does not record findings of fact, but rather allegations of fact following an investigation. In my view, it was not open to the Board to accept as fact the allegations contained in the police report without pointing to evidence or testimony to support an argument that on a balance of probabilities the police report characterizes the underlying facts in an accurate manner… 18Dhadwar v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety & Emergency Preparedness), 2008 FC 482 (F.C.) at para. 29.This is equivalent to a caution; i.e., police investigation, and therefore not a finding of fact reached by the Court. In fact, there is a significant difference between: 1) A person admitting guilt to a police officer; 2) A police officer issuing a caution after investigating the facts and deciding that the circumstances of the case do not require him to formally charge the person, and; 3) A person admitting guilt in a court of law after being asked to enter a plea.EquivalencyWhen conducting an equivalency analysis, the principles are well summarized in the often-quoted dicta in Hill v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration):[An equivalency analysis is to be conducted]… first, by a comparison of the precise wording in each statute both through documents and, if available, through the evidence of an expert or experts in the foreign law and determine there from the essential ingredients of the respective offences. Two, by examining the evidence adduced before the adjudicator, both oral and documentary, to ascertain whether or not that evidence was sufficient to establish the essential ingredients of the offence in Canada had been proven n the foreign proceedings, whether precisely described in the initiating documents or in the statutory provisions in the same words or not. Third, by a combination of one and two. 19Hill v. Canada (Minister of Employment & Immigration) (1987), 73 N.R. 315 (Fed. C.A.) at 320.In comparing the UK legislation to the Canadian Criminal Code, the line-by-line analysis is as follows:Wording of s. 39 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988Offences Wording of s. 267 of the Criminal CodeCommon assault and battery shall be summary offences and a person guilty of either of them shall be liable to a fine not exceeding level 5 on the standard scale, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, or to both.20https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1988/33/contents/2000-08-25. Note Level 5 was a maximum of £5,000 at the time.Assault causing bodily harm Every one who, in committing an assault, (b) causes bodily harm to the complainant, is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years or an offence punishable on summary conviction and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding eighteen months.
As such, although the essential elements are equivalent, a caution does not exist in Canadian criminal law.Additionally, in considering whether or not the applicant would be found guilty of a criminal offence in Canada given that they were intervening in what they believed to be a domestic violence assault, we would note that s. 30 of the Criminal Code states that “every one” — not just a peace officer — “who witnesses a breach of the peace is justified in interfering to prevent the continuance or renewal thereof.” It reads:30.Every one who witnesses a breach of the peace is justified in interfering to prevent the continuance or renewal thereof and may detain any person who commits or is about to join in or to renew the breach of the peace, for the purpose of giving him into the custody of a peace officer, if he uses no more force than is reasonably necessary to prevent the continuance or renewal of the breach of the peace or than is reasonably proportioned to the danger to be apprehended from the continuance or renewal of the breach of the peace.As well, consider the Criminal Code at s. 34:34.(1)A person is not guilty of an offence if(a)they believe on reasonable grounds that force is being used against them or another person or that a threat of force is being made against them or another person;(b)the act that constitutes the offence is committed for the purpose of defending or protecting themselves or the other person from that use or threat of force; and(c)the act committed is reasonable in the circumstances.(2)Marginal note: Factors—In determining whether the act committed is reasonable in the circumstances, the court shall consider the relevant circumstances of the person, the other parties and the act, including, but not limited to, the following factors:(a)the nature of the force or threat;(b)the extent to which the use of force was imminent and whether there were other means available to respond to the potential use of force;(c)the person's role in the incident;(d)whether any party to the incident used or threatened to use a weapon;(e)the size, age, gender and physical capabilities of the parties to the incident;(f)the nature, duration and history of any relationship between the parties to the incident, including any prior use or threat of force and the nature of that force or threat;(f.1)any history of interaction or communication between the parties to the incident;(g)the nature and proportionality of the person's response to the use or threat of force; and(h)whether the act committed was in response to a use or threat of force that the person knew was lawful.What is even more probable, in terms of equivalency, is that s. 730 of the Criminal Code provides that in a case where an accused person pleads guilty or is found guilty of certain offences, the court is empowered, instead of convicting the accused, to direct that he or she be discharged absolutely or upon conditions. Section 730(3) states that, except for certain defined purposes, when such a discharge is directed the offender shall be deemed not to have been convicted.In the immigration context, there is case law decided under the former immigration legislation in which the Federal Court determined that in cases where a person obtains a discharge, that person is not convicted of an offence. 21Lew v. Canada (Minister of Manpower & Immigration) (1974), 20 C.C.C. (2d) 127 (Fed. C.A.); Kalicharan v. Canada (Minister of Manpower & Immigration), [1976] 2 F.C. 123 (Fed. T.D.). This jurisprudence is arguably applicable under the current IRPA. This appears, in comparing the legislation, to be similar to a UK caution, but not equivalent given that the facts of the case were not tried in a court of law as they would be where a judge (and not a police officer) issues a discharge.Defences — Self DefenceA person may use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances in self-defence or defence of another, the defence of property, or the prevention of crime. The prosecution must prove that the use of force was unreasonable, which involves two questions: whether the use of any force was reasonably necessary in the circumstances and whether the amount of force used was excessive.Under Canadian law, if a case such as this had proceeded to trial, it is reasonable to find that the applicant would likely be acquitted on the grounds of self-defence or accidental striking of the victim of the assault. If there is no equivalency of defences and the defences available in Canada are broader than those available in a foreign jurisdiction, this could result in a finding that there is no equivalency.Humanitarian and Compassionate SubmissionThe applicant has become greatly integrated in Canada. To refuse this appeal, finding that he is inadmissible, and thereby separating this couple, would mean they would be separated indefinitely as there is no period of rehabilitation for a caution. His wife would be forced to forfeit her career and be separated from all of her family and friends, to leave all the people behind who depend on her for her support and start anew. This would cause significant hardship to her.Sample ConclusionThus, to summarize:1The commission provisions in the IRPA target serious criminal perpetrators that elude prosecution. None of those factors are present here and as such, the section is being misapplied. The first officer's assessment with respect, was a correct application of the law. The application by the SIO was not — see IRCC manuals providing guidance on how to apply the law.2The police did not lay a charge.3The offences have the same intent element and the same threshold for finding bodily harm (more than transient or trifling).4A discharge (conditional or absolute) can only follow a finding of guilt.5With a caution there is no formal plea.6The matter does not even go before a judge.7Further, preventing a crime and protecting another person is a valid defence to this charge. So while the applicant may have acknowledged the assault, he did not have an opportunity to explain that he was preventing a crime.8He had no criminal record prior to this incident.9He has no criminal record since the incident.10His life has been placed in an untenable position for a lengthy period and his lifestyle, relationship, and establishment all warrant the exercise of positive discretion.For relevant case law discussing equivalency analyses, see Appendix “C”.

Nonetheless, how these individuals enter the criminal justice stream will require a deeper analysis on how systemic racism operates at multiple levels and permeates society. While the pardon system may look to the past regime for setting parameters to assess future applications, looking to the past should end there.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold>Background – Race and Policing in Canada</bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">The over conviction and incarceration of racialized peoples in Canada is the result of systemic racial injustices existing across multiple systems, including the immigration system. This includes the immigration system. Without comprehensive efforts at dismantling these systems, Black individuals in this country will continue to face the negative impacts of systemic racism, which include criminalization but also poverty, under education, and (most importantly for the discussion herein) deportation as an extension of the criminal justice system. To draw out this argument, the within canvases the ways in which anti-Black racism has influenced the development of immigration legislation over the past thirty years. This will hopefully demonstrate how Blackness has been tied to dangerousness, and then used to justify increasingly punitive immigration legislation around migrant inadmissibility following a criminal conviction.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><ital>Criminal Inadmissibility and Race – 1994 to 2002</ital></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Most readers will know of the history of racist immigration legislation in Canada, including the <ital>Chinese Immigration Act,</ital> the internment of Japanese Canadians and the bar against the migration of Black persons on the basis that they were not suited to the “Canadian climate”.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">8</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Hawkins, Freda (1991). Critical years in immigration: Canada and Australia compared. Montreal: McGill-Queen's University Press.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> In a first attempt to move beyond these racist discourses and pieces of legislation, in the 1960s the Canada Government made the effort to remove any overtly racist materials from immigration legislation.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">9</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">For further information, see: <cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc85c50eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Pratt, Anna (2005). Montreal: McGill-Queen's University Press; Armenta, A. (2017)</ref></cite>. <cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc85c52eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">“Racializing Crimmigration: Structural Racism, Colorblindness and the Institutional Production of Immigrant Criminality”. Sociology of Race and Ethnicity, 3.1, pgs. 82-92</ref></cite>; and <cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc85c53eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Albrecht, H. (1997). “Ethnic Minorities, Crime and Criminal Justice in Germany.” Crime & Justice, 21, pgs. 31-100</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> It is on the historical period that follows these efforts to address racism that I will focus, in order to uncover the <ital>systemic</ital> ways in which racism continues to inflect our legislation and political discourse. I want to begin specifically by bringing the reader back to the Bill C-44, which was brought to Parliament in June 1994.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Bill C-44 included provisions that would remove the right of appeal from permanent residents found inadmissible for criminality who had been issued a certificate by the Minister of Immigration identifying them as a “danger to the public”.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">10</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Bill C-44, An Act to amend the Immigration Act and the Citizenship Act and to make a consequential amendment to the Customs Act, 1995, c. 15, section 9.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> In support of this legislation, then Minister Sergio Marchi pointed to the actions of a purported “criminal element” he claimed had “infiltrated” the immigration system, thereby causing Canadian “citizens” to question the “merits” of the system.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">11</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Canada, Parliament (19 September 1994). <cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc88360eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">House of Commons Debates, 35th Parl, 1st Sess. He stated: “We simply have to fix the system … to prevent <ital>thugs</ital> from using red tape or muddled intra-government communications to extend their stay in Canada.”<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">12</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Canada, Parliament (19 September 1994). <cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc8aa70eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">House of Commons Debates, 35th Parl, 1st Sess. Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 1994</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Prior to these amendments, permanent residents found inadmissible for serious criminality under the <ital>Immigration Act</ital> retained the right of appeal to the Immigration Appeal Division regardless of the offence for which they were convicted and/or their sentence. Bill C-44 thus introduced the first legislated limitations on access to appeal and the extension of Ministerial discretion over migrant inadmissibility for serious criminality, thereby ushering in the current removal regime. Following the enactment of Bill C-44 in July 1995, an individual found inadmissible for serious criminality could be determined to be a “danger to the public” by the Minister (really, a delegate of the Minister) marking an important shift from a transparent process to one that is more subjective and determinative of future risk. The Minister would base their exercise of discretion on a review of documentary evidence, as well as any submissions from the permanent resident, including those that referenced humanitarian and compassionate grounds against removal.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">13</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc8aa71eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Haigh, Richard and Jim Smith (1998). “Return of the Chancellor's Foot?: Discretion in Permanent Resident Deportation Appeals under the Immigration Act”. Journal of Prisoners on Prisons, vol. 28(1)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">While Marchi held that these provisions were not the result of an “overreaction to a few isolated incidents”, the tabling of this legislation followed two highly publicized events in Toronto: the death of Georgina Leimonis during the <ital>Just Desserts</ital> shootings and the death of Todd Baylis.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">14</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc8d180eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Hawkins, Freda (1991). Critical years in immigration: Canada and Australia compared. Montreal: McGill-Queen's University Press</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> The media identified the perpetrators of the offences in the events as Black, Jamaican men. The media further stated that these individuals were <bold>not</bold> citizens of Canada and that they were not legally in the country. Clinton Gayle, who was eventually convicted of the shooting death of Todd Baylis, was erroneously identified by the media as having evaded removal following the issuance of a deportation order against him based on his previous criminal convictions.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">15</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc8d181eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Pratt, Anna (2005). Similarly, while the men involved in the Just Desserts offences were identified as being non-citizens, in fact they were all permanently residing in Canada. One individual who was associated with the events (Oneil Grant) was identified as being a temporary migrant to the country; however, Grant was later exonerated of all charges.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">16</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc8d182eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">CBC News, “Man cleared in Just Desserts case killed in Jamaica”, 5 November 2007</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The need to remove “dangerous” Black, Jamaican men was oft-repeated in the promotion of Bill C-44. For example, then Member of Parliament Art Hanger stated the following in supporting the new enforcement initiatives during debates of the Bill:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>First is the much publicized case of Clinton Gayle who is suspected of the murder of Constable Todd Baylis. Mr. Gayle came to the country legally. Mr. Gayle had a removal order issued against him. Mr. Gayle evaded that deportation order not by running and not by tying up the system with appeals. Rather, Mr. Gayle avoided removal because his file was lost. Mr. Gayle avoided capture and removal because the system was over worked, because priorities for removal were confused. It is more likely than not, although we will never know, because someone dropped the ball.</ital></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold><ital>[…]</ital></bold></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>The second case that has outraged Canadians and has illustrated the deficiencies both in immigration and in the priorities of this government was the very recent case of one Mr. Forbes. He is currently being sought for the senseless shooting of several people in Toronto over the weekend.</ital></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>Tragically two of those people died at the hands of this individual. <bold>Mr. Forbes who is also from Jamaica</bold> came to Canada on a visitor's visa, as so many illegal entrants do. He overstayed that visa and a deportation order was issued.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">17</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc8f890eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Canada, Parliament (22 September 1994). Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 1994</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></ital></para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Similarly, MP Sharon Hayes noted the necessity of the legislation, citing the death of Todd Baylis specifically and the ongoing threat faced by police officers given the limits of immigration enforcement. MP Hayes tied this threat to Black, Jamaican men in Canada, stating:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>…this weekend in a national news report… it was reported that Canada returned 227 deportees to <bold>Jamaica</bold> from January to July of this year, one-quarter of the total from all sources. It also pointed out that wealthy countries such as Canada are viewed by some countries as dumping our problems on them.</ital></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>[…]</ital></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>We need to equip those in the trenches not just with a book of rules but with the tools to do the job. We need to assure the shopkeepers, the businessmen, the parents and the police, <bold>Canadians</bold> by birth or by choice that they do not need to <bold>fear the system that should protect them.</bold></ital><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">18</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc91fa0eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Canada, Parliament (22 September 1994). House of Commons Debates, 35th Parl, 1st Sess. Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 1994</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">MP Hayes' statements clearly reflect the link between anti-Black racism, dangerousness, enforcement and the hyper-surveillance of Black bodies in Canada.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">19</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc91fa1eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Henry, F., & Tator, C. (2002). Discourses of domination: Racial bias in the Canadian English-language press. Toronto: University of Toronto Press</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> These authors characterized the Just Desserts case in particular as revealing of the “powerful examples of newer forms of racism, such as those that invoke the supposed inferiority of ‘foreign’ cultures”.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">20</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc946b0eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Henry, F., & Tator, C. (2002). Discourses of domination: Racial bias in the Canadian English-language press. Toronto: University of Toronto Press pg. 168</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> Jamaica and its citizens are characterized by Hayes, MP Hanger, and even Minister Marchi as uncooperative, refusing to accept the return of men who pose a threat to Canada and its citizens. The Just Desserts case became a symbol of anti-immigration rhetoric, in which Jamaican men and Black people are positioned as always dangerous, always criminal, and always non-citizen.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Importantly for the discussion herein, and according to Dr. Anna Pratt of York University<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">21</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc946b1eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Canada, Parliament (19 September 1994). House of Commons Debates, 35th Parl, 1st Sess. Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 1994</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> (2005), as a result of this change in legislation and restrictions on the right of appeal, Black male migrants faced the compounding impact of discrimination in both the immigration and criminal justice systems. Specifically, because of these amendments, decisions of police, prosecutors and judges became central to administrative determinations of dangerousness. Danger decisions would, as a result, necessarily reproduce the individual and systemic racisms and discrimination that marred the operations and practices of the criminal justice system (as had at that point been clearly determined by Stephen Lewis in his report for the Ontario government).<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">22</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfc946b2eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Canada, Parliament (19 September 1994). Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 1994</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold><ital>Deportation post Bill C-44 and pre-IRPA</ital></bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Research on deportations post-1994 confirms that Black folks in Canada are at a greater risk of removal. This is a significant reduction from the previous legislation, which again allowed access to appeal for migrants sentenced to a term of imprisonment of two years or less.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">In review of the debates of this legislation before Parliament, we again see the use of narratives relying on anti-Black racism to justify the increasingly punitive legislative amendments. For example, Minister Jason Kenney, the sponsor of the Bill, referenced the incidents in Toronto in 1994 as justification for the legislation, namely the shooting at Just Desserts and the death of Todd Baylis. Minister Kenney stated that “foreign criminals” are able to “walk freely on our streets when they should have been sent home at the earliest opportunity”, as evidenced by the death of Todd Baylis, who Kenney stated was “killed by a foreign national who was delaying his deportation”.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">49</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Canada, Parliament (24 October 2012). <cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfcb1b70eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Standing Committee on Citizenship and Immigration, 41st Parl, 1st Sess. Jamaican men are positioned as non-citizens who threaten Canadians and abuse our systems.
