In his submissions before the Standing Committee on 31 October 2012, Tom Stamatakis from the Canadian Police Association similarly stated that Mr. Baylis died following his encounter with “Jamaican born Clinton Gayle” who was at that point a “veteran drug trafficker” with “a fully loaded nine-millimeter handgun and pockets filled with bags of crack cocaine”, again tying Black men to foreignness and criminality.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">51</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Canada, Parliament (31 October 2012). <cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfcb4280eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Standing Committee on Citizenship and Immigration, 41st Parl, 1st Sess. Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 2012</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> Mr. Stamatakis held that the legislative amendments were necessary to ensure that similar tragedies did not befall police officers in particular in the future.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Debates of the <ital>FRFCA</ital> again saw discussion of the impact that the legislative amendments would specifically have on Black male migrants. For example, during the second reading of the Bill before the House of Commons, MP Mike Sullivan from the NDP held that the legislation would directly affect the Somali youth in his riding (York South-Weston) who may have been in Canada for their entire lives but, because of their experiences with criminalization, would now face deportation to a country they did not know and that continues to struggle with civil war.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">52</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Canada, Parliament (24October 2012). <cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfcb4281eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">House of Commons Debates, 41st Parl, 1st Sess. Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 2012</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> These youth were described as having little support in Canada, including from the Canadian government in terms of settlement services, which had been cut under the Conservative party.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">MP Sullivan compared the experiences of the young Black men in his riding to that of Conrad Black, a wealthy white man convicted of criminal offences who was allowed to enter Canada even after the imposition of a 14-year sentence against him. In drawing these connections, MP Sullivan makes clear that the legislation proposed would have a specific negative impact on Black youth in Canada, given the ongoing social context that deprives them of economic and social support and subjects them to increased enforcement measures in both the immigration and criminal justice systems.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">53</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Canada, Parliament (24October 2012). <cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfcb4282eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">House of Commons Debates, 41st Parl, 1st Sess. Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 2012</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Ahmed Hussen of the Canadian Somali Congress similarly expressed concern that the bill would lead to the deportation of young Somali men during debate before the Standing Committee on 21 November 2012.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">54</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Canada, Parliament (21 November 2012). <cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfcb6990eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Standing Committee on Citizenship and Immigration, 41st Parl, 1st Sess. Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 2012</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> Mr. Hussen was not challenged on this position. However, when Mr. Francisco Rico-Martinez (Regional Director of the Ontario Council of Agencies Serving Immigrants) presented the position that the legislation would have a disproportionate impact on Black and racialized permanent residents of Canada, he was met with significant pushback from the opposing Conservative party.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">55</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Canada, Parliament (21 November 2012). <cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfcb6991eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Standing Committee on Citizenship and Immigration, 41st Parl, 1st Sess. Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 2012</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Mr. Rico-Martinez testified at the Standing Committee on 19 November 2012. During his speech, Rico-Martinez noted the ties between the immigration and criminal justice systems, including where the over policing of Black men would contribute to their greater likelihood of deportation. He stated:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>A 2010 Toronto Star investigative series on Toronto police data for the period 2003 to 2008 found that black men ages 15 to 24 years are stopped and documented 2.5 times more than white males the same age. The finding echoed a similar analysis of data the Toronto Star conducted in 2002.</ital></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>The overrepresentation of visible minorities in the prison system is rooted in factors of poverty, economic inequality, and historical prejudice. That includes the over-policing of young black men, a practice that results in racial profiling. The existence of racial profiling by police is well documented. It has been acknowledged to different degrees by various police services in Canada, including the Kingston police chief in 2005.</ital></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>[…]</ital></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>Individuals who have lived all their lives in Canada, particularly those who came as infants or young children, would lose families, friends and communities when they are deported to a place they barely know or remember from before. They will have no family or community connections over there. Unlike Canadian citizens, permanent residents will be punished twice for committing a crime.</ital><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">56</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfcb90a0eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Canada, Parliament (19 October 2012). Standing Committee on Citizenship and Immigration, 41st Parl, 1st Sess. Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 2012</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Unfortunately, Mr. Rico-Martinez's position was ultimately dismissed, including by Roxanne James, MP for the Conservative party, who held that the witness was “making excuses for people who commit crime”, and that there are many people who “fit those categories” identified by Rico-Martinez as being subjected to increased enforcement who “do not commit serious crimes”.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">57</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="secondary"><ref ref.id="Ibfcb90a1eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" short="y">Canada, Parliament (19 October 2012). Standing Committee on Citizenship and Immigration, 41st Parl, 1st Sess. Ottawa: Canadian Government Publishing, 2012</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">By deploying discourses that tie criminality to exclusively rational choice, MP James dismissed the consideration of the contribution of the social context to the over criminalization of Black people in Canada, as identified not only by Mr. Rico-Martinez but several other witnesses since 1994. Again, this dismissal by James tied Blackness to an inherent dangerousness, where Black people are not over policed and over incarcerated because of systemic racial biases that continue to mar our systems, but because of their own rational choices.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Perhaps more than ever, with the passage of Bill C-43 the ties between Blackness, dangerousness and foreignness have been clearly established in discourses that justified the restrictions on access to appeal in the administrative immigration system. Discussions of the practical implications of the limitations on rights of appeal within the immigration system for Black Canadians continued within the decision of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Tran" p2="Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)" post.rptr="50" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="Ibfcbb7b0eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" title="Tran v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)">Tran v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2017 SCC 50 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Tran sought to overturn the decision of the Minister's delegate referring his matter to an admissibility hearing before the Immigration Division on the basis that he was inadmissible to Canada for serious criminality. Interveners in the matter on behalf of Tran included the African Canadian Legal Clinic. Factum materials from this intervener drew attention to two specific arguments on the impact of deportation for Black migrants specifically: 1) the decision in question would have a significant negative impact on the Black population in Canada given that more than half of this group are migrants, with a large proportion holding only permanent residence; and 2) Black people in Canada are racially profiled and overpoliced, resulting in their disproportionate representation in police stop data.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">On the secondary point in particular, the ACLC highlighted that delegates of the Minister deciding to refer for inadmissibility may rely on non-conviction records. This happened in Tran and was characterized as “standard practice”. The ACLC asked the Court to find this practice unacceptable, given that it is well established in legal and academic communities that Black individuals are “routinely and systematically subjected to racial profiling by police”. This has been demonstrated, for example, through multiple studies examining both carding practices and traffic stops (Toronto Star, Wortley 2005 study, etc.). Because Black individuals are racially profiled and subject to over-policing, the ACLC argued that they are “disproportionately represented in police stop data and are more susceptible to non- conviction records.” Additionally, these records are largely comprised of an officer's subjective account of their interaction with the member of the public. They may thus include “untested and unproven allegations to which no measure of reliability should attach”.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In support of their position, the ACLC drew from the work of Scot Wortley on the connection between immigration and crime to highlight the impact of the use of non-conviction records on Black populations in Canada. Here, the ACLC discussed how immigration law and decision making on deportation reproduces systemic racisms inherent in the criminal justice system by using criminal justice materials that are built on, and perpetuate, discrimination against Black peoples. The ACLC stated that:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>… the deportation of Black noncitizens who are convicted of less serious criminal offences also serves to perpetuate the position of disadvantage faced by this community. For most, the prospect of deportation to their country of birth is even more frightening than a term of imprisonment. Like the Appellant, many Black permanent residents have spent the majority of their lives in Canada and have established deep roots in this country. The financial and emotional well-being of their families requires them to remain in Canada. Many have not returned since their emigration and so upon repatriation they languish in unfamiliar surroundings alienated from their families and support networks.</ital><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">58</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">These materials were requested from the Supreme Court of Canada. For further information, see: <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="Ibfcbb7b1eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8">https://www.scc-csc.ca/case-dossier/info/search-recherche-eng.aspx</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The use of non-conviction records as evidence supporting a determination of serious criminality was argued by the ACLC to be not only unreliable but dangerous. The ACLC thus asked that the Supreme Court of Canada issue a finding clearly stating that the Minister's use of these records was unacceptable as it “relied uncritically on the policing and enforcement practices of the criminal justice system and failed to consider the systemic anti-Black racism that traverses that system”.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">59</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">These materials were requested from the Supreme Court of Canada. For further information, see: <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="Ibfcbdec0eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8">https://www.scc-csc.ca/case-dossier/info/search-recherche-eng.aspx</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Regrettably, the Supreme Court made no mention of this issue in its decision. Still, what the Tran case demonstrates is the ongoing and significant impact of decisions limiting rights of appeal for Black individuals in Canada. While not directly relevant to s. 64(2), what Tran and the ACLC materials highlight is the intimate interweaving of the immigration and criminal justice system in determinations of serious criminality. This intersection can be found as early as the initial decision to refer in the immigration system, with the Minister's delegate drawing from criminal court materials to support their discretionary decision-making process.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">As was oft warned in legislative debates, these practices in turn introduce systemic racisms inherent in the criminal justice system into the immigration system, with materials that draw from discrimination against Black people used to further exclude and remove these individuals from Canada. Where Black migrants do retain the right of appeal, as was demonstrated by Dr. Chan, they are less likely to receive favourable decisions on their appeal.</para.text></para><head align="l" toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><name date.updated="0"><bold><ital>Pardon Regime</ital></bold></name></name.block></head><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">To return to Bill C-31 and the effort to change access to pardons. As stated at the outset, these efforts are commendable. For migrants deported from Canada for serious criminality, it could mean that they will be reunited with their family members sooner than anticipated. This is particularly important given the breadth of offences now caught by the <ital>IRPA</ital> for deportation.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">The problem remains, though, that systemic racism inflects all of our systems. Black and racialized migrants are oversurveilled, overpoliced and over incarcerated. The immigration removal system has been in part built on the basis of their deportation. While it is good news that migrants will now have access to reprieve from their criminal convictions, these migrants will continue to face deportation in the first instance. They will continue to face the adverse consequences of racism that is inherent within all of our legislation. Without change that addresses these more foundational issues, we will continue to see the same people being sent to prison, and subsequently removed from Canada.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">For permanent residents charged and convicted in Canada, the eligibility to apply and receive more expedient pardons could bypass the entire inadmissibility process for some and avoid the collateral consequence of deportation following a conviction which would reduce the number of potential appeals to the IAD. This is particularly acute given how long the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) writes and refers a section 44 report following a conviction in Canada.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">As per section 44 of the <underscore><ital>IRPA</ital></underscore>:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">44 (1) An officer who is of the opinion that a permanent resident or a foreign national who is in Canada is inadmissible may prepare a report setting out the relevant facts, which report shall be transmitted to the Minister.</para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">(2) If the Minister is of the opinion that the report is well-founded, the Minister may refer the report to the Immigration Division for an admissibility hearing…</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Paragraph 36(1)(a) of the <underscore><ital>IRPA</ital></underscore> provides:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">36 (1) A permanent resident or a foreign national is inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality for</para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">(a) having been convicted in Canada of an offence under an Act of Parliament punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years, or of an offence under an Act of Parliament for which a term of imprisonment of more than six months has been imposed;</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Again, as a result of the coming into force of section 24 of the <underscore><ital>Faster Removal of Foreign Criminals Act</ital></underscore>, SC 2013, c 16 (<underscore><ital>FRFCA</ital></underscore>) section 64 of the <underscore><ital>IRPA</ital></underscore> cited above provides that no appeal to the IAD is available for a permanent resident who has been found inadmissible for serious criminality, where a term of imprisonment of at least six months has been imposed. A more expeditious pardon regime could assist Canadian permanent residents from becoming inadmissible. The CBSA in many instances has taken years to act on preparing section 44 reports so permanent residents who had access to the IAD at the time of the conviction and for years following by the time the report was referred no longer had access to the IAD.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In <underscore>Granados v. Canada</underscore><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">60</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Granados" p2="Canada (M.C.I.)" post.rptr="302" pre.rptr="2018" ref.id="Ibfcc05d0eec111eb86ccd59fa0a33ae8" title="Granados v. Canada (M.C.I.)">Granados v. Canada (M.C.I.), 2018 FC 302 paras. 1-4, 58</ref></cite> [<underscore>Granados</underscore>].</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> the Applicant sought judicial review of the decision of the IAD which dismissed the Applicant's appeal of a deportation order issued by the Immigration Division (ID) for lack of jurisdiction. The Honourable Justice Russell concluded that the Applicant should have sought judicial review of the ID decision as in the case at bar:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">[58] One of the problems with these allegations is that the unfairness and “reaching back” issues and the fairness and equitable arguments could all have been raised in judicial review proceedings dealing with the referral decision of November 7, 2016 or the deportation order of January 11, 2017. Yet the Applicant, for no reason that he now places before the Court (he has filed no affidavit), decided not to challenge them. He has chosen, instead, to challenge the IAD's jurisdiction decision on grounds that Parliament could not have intended an extensive or open-ended reach back effect when it enacted s 64 of the <underscore><ital>IRPA</ital></underscore>.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Even in cases like <underscore>Granados</underscore> where the CBSA's delay in bringing forward the inadmissibility allegation was unreasonable, unexplained and unjustified and even where the delay was caused exclusively by the CBSA the Immigration Appeal Division was deemed to have no jurisdiction even for abuse of process arguments. In that case it was open to the CBSA to bring forward an inadmissibility allegation many years ago. The CBSA's decision when to forward the report and referral to the ID was a matter entirely outside the Applicant's control. Yet the Federal Court found the Appellant should have raised the issue much earlier at the referral stage or at the ID stage.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Interestingly, the Respondent highlighted in the <underscore>Granados</underscore> matter that CBSA policy is to send a permanent resident who has been convicted of a serious criminal offence a warning letter when the Minister's Delegate believes the report to be well-founded but decides not to refer the report to the ID. The warning letter advises “<ital>that a decision could be made to refer the report at a later date</ital>” and is intended to have a deterring effect. The Court in that matter determined this was highly relevant at paragraph 33:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">[33] Here, the Applicant was warned that the CBSA was aware of his first conviction and was put on notice that reoffending could result in his deportation. So there is no settled expectation of the Applicant that has been interfered with and there is no evidence that the Applicant would have acted differently had he known that he could not appeal the issuance of a deportation order to the IAD.</para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The Federal Court, in <underscore>Granados</underscore>, noted the scope of legal arguments that could have been raised at paragraph 60:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>The Applicant's failure to challenge earlier decisions, where he could have raised any humanitarian and compassionate factors and all of the equitable and fairness arguments he has raised before me, cannot be used as a basis for arguing that Parliament's failure to limit the “reach back” consequence of s 64 means that Parliament's intent was unclear.</ital></para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In these types of cases, decade long delays in writing and referring reports makes the changes to the pardon regime all the more important, as eligibility for a pardon may ultimately delay or completely forestall the pursuit of a deportation order for those caught by section 64 or otherwise. The elimination of a right of appeal that profoundly impairs a permanent resident's ability to challenge his removal from Canada is in most cases life altering. As the discussion above highlights, these consequences are visited upon racialized permanent residents disproportionately. The suggested amendments are the first of many steps required to undo years of genericizing the inadmissibility process. The next step should look to reversing boilerplate growing obstacles like the ever-encroaching section 64 of the <underscore>IRPA</underscore> prohibiting in many cases permanent residents who have lived in Canada for decades from receiving an individualized assessment of their circumstances before being deported. Relying on section 25 of the <underscore>IRPA</underscore> in the place of a full appeal is as hollow as the statistics that fueled section 64.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:27: <section date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124" date.revised="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:27</designator><name date.updated="0">New <ital>IAD Rules</ital> set out procedures to facilitate early resolution, and reflect realities of working in a digital era</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The previous version of the <ital>IAD Rules</ital>, introduced in 2002 were in much need of an overhaul. While the practice of immigration law has evolved over the years, nothing came as a greater catalyst for change than the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced everyone in the industry to adapt in order to survive. On a positive note, this had the benefit of encouraging “updates” to the way things had been done for decades, which proved to be more efficient, convenient, and inclusive than ever before with the massive shift to adopting technology that has been around for years to help us all accomplish our work.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The <ital>Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement</ital> issued by the IRB with respect to the <ital>IAD Rules</ital> sets out the issues that were identified with the previous version of the <ital>IAD Rules</ital> introduced in 2002, including:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The 2002 IAD Rules established time limits that resulted in undue delays in considering an appeal. For example, the time limit for the Minister to provide an appeal record in sponsorship and residency obligation appeals was 120 days. In most cases, this time limit prevented any processing of the appeal during that time since the appeal record contains all the documents used to make the decision being appealed as well as the reasons for that decision.</bold></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The procedures for disclosure of documents in the 2002 IAD Rules were oriented to support formal hearings and they did not facilitate informal resolution outcomes or hearing preparedness. The 2002 IAD Rules required disclosure 20 days before the hearing which limited the ability for the Immigration Appeal Division (IAD) and parties to identify possible areas of resolution or procedural issues that might have needed additional attention before setting a hearing date. In the process set out in the 2002 IAD Rules, the IAD had to ask the parties for information to support informal resolution activities, which often resulted in the parties having to provide disclosure (additional information) at multiple stages in their appeal, initially for informal resolution and then later for their hearing.</bold></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The procedures set out in the 2002 IAD Rules made it difficult for the IAD to provide timely procedural support to self-represented appellants. Despite efforts to prepare appellants before scheduling a hearing, many appellants still appeared for their hearing inadequately prepared since the 2002 IAD Rules required documents and other information for the proceeding to be provided 20 days before the hearing. Identifying appellants requiring additional procedural guidance and providing that guidance just weeks before a scheduled hearing was impractical and often impossible. This created a barrier to access to justice for these appellants as well as inefficiencies in scheduling appeals, which could delay deciding other appeals. The 2002 IAD Rules could also have benefited from more organization and clearer language to support appellants navigating the process without legal representation.</bold></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The 2002 IAD Rules were dated and required standard updates to reflect current realities and previous recommendations. The 2002 IAD Rules needed to better reflect electronic practices that improve efficiency and client service, address recommendations made by the Standing Joint Committee for the Scrutiny of Regulations, and where appropriate, align common processes with the Rules of other Divisions at the IRB.</bold><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Government of Canada, “Immigration Appeal Division Rules, 2022: SOR/2022-277”, online: <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="I235c44e07a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45">https://www.gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p2/2023/2023-01-04/html/sor-dors277-eng.html</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Bellissimo Law Group PC was invited to weigh-in on proposed changes to the <ital>IAD Rules</ital> and provided recommendations to the IRB on 11 July 2022. Included in our comments were the following twenty-five general recommendations, in addition to more specific feedback on proposed changes:</para.text><list list.style="block" be resolved in a manner that is consistent with the “interests of justice.”</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator
