considered.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>4</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>There is a need for clarification on the format of notice of appeals.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>5</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>All available information must be included in the Appeal Record.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>6</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The proposed 45-day timeline for production of materials could have significant, and potentially actionable, consequences.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>7</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Translator's declaration should include a declaration of “no conflict.”</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>8</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Measures should be undertaken to divert mentally disordered appellants from the removal process.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>9</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Language must be consistent across the <ital>Rules.</ital></bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>10</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Interpreter's declaration should include a declaration of “no conflict.”</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>11</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The required provision of witness information and disclosure within the 45-day timeline could have significant, and again actionable, consequences.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>12</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Further clarity is required regarding confidentiality of materials filed in informal resolution processes.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>13</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Further guidelines are required regarding who can function as an ADR conference facilitator.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>14</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>All parties should have the opportunity to request a “conference.”</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>15</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Hearings should follow the principles of justice and the rule of law.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>16</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Qualify time limits for change of location of hearings to include “within fifteen days of receipt of the Notice of Appeal.”</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>17</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Qualify time limits for changing the date and/or time of a proceeding to include “within fifteen days of receipt of the Notice of Appeal.”</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>18</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The test of “exceptional circumstances” for changing date/time/location of a hearing must be clarified.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>19</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Additional guidelines must be provided with respect to the threshold test for assessment of claims of inadequate counsel.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>20</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Decisions of the Division should only be given orally if they are positive and only if the Respondent is present.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>21</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Retrospective application of the <ital>Rules</ital> will offend the rule of law.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>22</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Change reference to “counsel” in Schedule to “Authorized Representative.”</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>23</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The <ital>Rules</ital> should allow for identification and review of multiple issues of inadmissibility on appeal.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>24</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Information on authorized representatives provided on the IRB's website should be neutral.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>25</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The IRB should provide more comprehensive information, including legal resources and up-to-date policy decisions, on its webpage.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Bellissimo Law Group PC's more rule-specific feedback included:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 1 – Definitions</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>1</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Many <ital>Rules</ital> are impacted by a lack of clarity and simplicity, including R59(2), 72(1), 79(1), 85(1), 86(1), 87 (1), 93(2), and 104. To this end, we recommend that terms like “in writing” and “written request” be defined in the <ital>Rules</ital> and include electronic filing. There should additionally be better cross-referencing to Rules 35 to 41 as including documents filed “in writing”. This would be easier to follow.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 3 - No Applicable Rule</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>2</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>In addition to resolving appeals <ital>effectively, completely, and fairly,</ital> this rule should include in the <ital>interests of justice</ital> as an identifiable legal test.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 11 - Request to be Removed as Counsel of Record</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>3</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>It is not clear whether Rules 11(1), (2), and (3) contemplate situations where there arises a conflict of interest between a lawyer and the appellant and/or the applicant. In this instance, the lawyer cannot provide a written request to be removed; the lawyer would have to remove themselves simply and automatically from representation. While we understand this Rule may be designed to protect the interests of the public, it does not envision scenarios where a lawyer cannot even divulge the reason for seeking removal. The Rule as it stands is too restrictive and could result in prejudice to appellants, applicants, and lawyers.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 14 and 15 – Filing an Appeal</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>4.</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>It is recommended that the format(s) in which an appeal can be filed (i.e., electronically, in writing, by facsimile, etc.) be clarified in Rules 14 and 15 by referencing Rules 35 to 41.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 20 - Appeal Record</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>5</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The word “relevant” should be removed as a qualifier to the documents the Minister is required to disclose in Rules 20(1)(d), 20(3)(c) and 20(4)(b). Given the aim is to expedite proceedings, the Minister should be compelled to produce all information in its possession. Otherwise, appellants will be forced to resort to cumbersome <ital>Access to Information and Privacy Requests</ital> (ATIPS) to confirm that all information is before the IAD, which will inevitably delay the progress of the appeal.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 22 - Appeal Record Time</bold></para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>We endorse the shortened timelines to produce the Appeal Record. This will certainly speed up the process and, in the case of a sponsorship appeal, will assist with the anxiety appellants face due to separation from their family for prolonged periods.</bold></para.text></quote.para></quote.block></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 26 - Time limit for Disclosure of Evidence</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>6</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The 45 days condensed timeline is one we advocated for, but we are now concerned, however, that this timeline will impact practical efficacy if the hearing is not soon after. If a hearing is months away and there is no opportunity to provide updated disclosure given the <ital>de novo</ital> nature of the proceeding, it is unclear how this specified and restricted timeline will work and its legal enforceability. This date must still be tethered to the hearing date – i.e., now for example, 20 days before the hearing.</bold></para.text><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>It will be onerous for authorized representatives to review the record, identify the issues/areas of concern, collect, and review all documents provided, and finalize the disclosure, especially if the appeal record is incomplete and/or contains only “relevant” information, as determined by the Minister. This 45-day rule to submit disclosure seems to be overridden only in cases where the disclosure is being provided for the Informal Resolution Process (Rule 24(2)). This will result in multiple filings; one within 45 days of receipt of the appeal record and then another 30 days before the hearing, which must include an explanation/justification of why the materials were not provided within the initial 45-day timeline. Also, as to Rule 29, the risk of the appeal being considered abandoned if the disclosure is not provided within 45 days of receipt of the appeal record reads as too restrictive and potentially unfair to appellants. Disclosure dates should be tied to both the production of the appeal record and the date of hearing. One does not work without the other.</bold></para.text><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Finally, if the appeal is not resolved informally before proceeding to the hearing, and the hearing is scheduled months after the disclosure is filed according to the new deadline proposed, this may again create more work for authorized representatives and the appellant if late disclosure must be filed with updated documents before the hearing.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 34 – Translator's Declaration</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>7</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>It is recommended that this declaration include a declaration of no conflict with any of the individuals party to the proceeding.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 41 - Extension of time limit — next working day</bold></para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>In practice, we have always acted that if a deadline for disclosure, etc., fell on a Saturday, it had to be filed the day before. This rule changes that practice and will ensure consistency with provisions of the Federal Court. We thus welcome this amendment.</bold></para.text></quote.para></quote.block></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 47 – Designated Representatives Factors to Consider</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>8</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>In the original IAD Innovation Plan</bold><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">2</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (March 2006). “IAD Innovation Plan”. <ital>Government of Canada.</ital></para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> <bold>it was provided that an effort would be made at phase three to introduce diversions of mentally disordered appellants from the removal order process. The reasoning behind this decisive step was to better handle sensitive cases and to allow them a just process. According to the report, “the IAD proposes to lay the foundation for a different approach to the management of mentally disordered persons who come into the immigration appeals process after having been ordered removed because of criminality.</bold><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">3</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (March 2006). “IAD Innovation Plan”. <ital>Government of Canada</ital>, pg. 28.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> <bold>Namely, individuals in this category would be merged into a stream with other appeal cases that guarantees special procedures and renders the system more just. This is an excellent recommendation, and the <ital>Rules</ital> should make provision for these opportunities.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 53 – “Interpreter”</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>9</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>We recommend consistent language across the <ital>Rules</ital>, including in the use of the term “translator.” Reference to the term “interpreter” should thus be removed. This will aid in avoiding confusion.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 54 – “Interpreter's” Oath</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>10</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Recommendation 7 would apply equally here, and a no conflict-of-interest declaration should be added to the oath. Following recommendation 9, above, the language of “interpreter” should be replaced with “translator”.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rules 55 and 56 – Witness Information and Failure to provide Witness Information</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>11</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Again, if an appeal is not scheduled in a timely fashion this mandate to produce disclosure and witnesses within the 45-day timeline will become difficult. Extension of time applications, special requests, etc., could become the norm. We appreciate that requiring disclosure and witness information be provided earlier in the process would potentially increase efficiency and reduce processing times. And it is argued that it would allow the IAD to be more efficient in scheduling hearings, since the IAD would be better able to determine the hearing duration required and to identify appeals that could benefit from a pre-hearing conference to ensure evidence is relevant to the issues in the appeal. Unless full appeal records are provided, however (as noted under recommendation 5), this <ital>Rule</ital> will not allow for receipt and review of the ATIPs, which is often needed on appeals as previous representatives sometimes cannot provide a complete copy of the underlying application materials <underscore>and</underscore> the Appeal Record is often incomplete. Depending on when the hearing is eventually scheduled, the witness may no longer be involved or available and this could be assessed negatively.</bold></para.text><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>These concerns are especially relevant to expert witnesses, given that: 1) time is required to identify an appropriate expert; (2) fees are often high, and appellants usually need time to pay or access the funds/participate in a payment plan, etc.; (3) appellants must usually attend appointments or examination by witnesses; and (4) a report must be written by the expert. This process can only be embarked upon if a hearing is imminent, and a fulsome Appeal Record has been provided. Although Rule 56 provides for an avenue to file the information after the 45-day timeline, it carries with it a legal test and therefore appears to be at the discretion of the Member. This complicates rather than simplifies the process.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 66 - Informal Resolution Process: Confidentiality of Discussions and Rule 67 Document Not Confidential</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>12</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>It is unclear if “<ital>any information</ital>” which could arise from a document filed subject to Rule 67 would be confidential or require a measure pursuant to section 166(b) of the <ital>Immigration and Refugee Protection Act</ital>? Further precision of language is required.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 70 – Assignment of ADR Conference Facilitator</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>13</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>What employees of the Board are eligible to function as ADR conference facilitators? Qualifying details of the type of employee and appropriate restrictions to ensure the individual has been trained and is competent should be codified. The Rule is simply too broad.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 72 – Conferences</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>14</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Based on a plain reading of Rule 72, it does not appear that a party can request a conference (other than an ADR conference). A pre-hearing conference identified by one of the parties can be a valuable tool to earlier resolution. The <ital>Rules</ital> should allow for such a request.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>R 74 – Conduct of a Hearing</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>15</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>It is recommended that hearings before the Division be guided by not only the <ital>nature and complexity of the issues</ital> but also by principles of fairness and the rule of law, and that any decisions taken are consistent with the <ital>Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms</ital>.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 88 - Changing Location</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>16</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>It is recommended this Rule be qualified to read “within fifteen days of receiving the Notice of Appeal.” Otherwise, if the Notice of Appeal is issued with less than or close to thirty days before the date of the hearing, the Rule becomes difficult to comply with in practice.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 90 - Changing Date or Time</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>17</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Same issue as set out in Recommendation 16.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 91 - Exceptional circumstances</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>18</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The threshold test of <ital>exceptional circumstances</ital> is neither defined nor reads as an extraordinary bar to satisfy. We recommend additional context and scope be added to the Rule considering that there may be legal reasons for a delay, including that a key document or report is still not available, a witness is not available, or a lawyer has been scheduled for a Federal Court appearance. It is unclear if any of these sometime routine occurrences could be described as exceptional.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 98 - Application to Re-open Appeal</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>19</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The threshold test of <ital>inadequate</ital> representation is not clearly defined in law and could potentially open a floodgate of allegations being made against former representatives/requests to re-open an appeal on this ground. It may have a chilling effect on authorized representatives' willingness to represent appellants, given the fear of such allegations being raised unreasonably and any potential consequences of these applications (e.g., complaints being made to regulators). It is strongly recommended that the Rule reference a protocol or <ital>Chairperson's Guideline,</ital> like the Federal Court Protocol on the Ineffective Assistance of Counsel</bold><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">4</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Chief Justice Paul Crampton (7 March 2014). “Re: Allegations Against Counsel or Other Representative in Citizenship, Immigration and Protected Person Cases before the Federal Court”. Federal Court of Canada. Please note that the Federal Court of Canada is currently in the process of updating this Protocol.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote><bold>, which sets out a series of procedural steps and safeguards to protect and respect all parties' interests. The Protocol is underscored by jurisprudence that establishes the requisite tests to satisfy. The Rule as it stands could raise considerable issues.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 104(b) - When Decision Takes Effect</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>20</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>It is strongly recommended that only positive decisions be rendered orally where at minimum the Respondent is represented. Otherwise, timelines for seeking relief at the Federal Court may be lost on appellants, which will raise procedural fairness issues that will only lead to a multiplicity of unnecessary proceedings.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Rule 105(1) - Transitional Proceedings</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>21</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>One of the key objectives underpinning this regulatory change is the application of a plain language lens to the <ital>Rules</ital>. Applying a retrospective application to most of the <ital>Rules</ital> severely undermines that objective. What is abundantly clear is that the rule of law ensures that individuals know the law to which they are subject, that laws are stable, predictable, and ordered. Individuals ought to be able to organize their lives in such a way that they can live in compliance with the law, which can only be achieved by law being known and new laws being applied prospectively. The same should apply to the <ital>Rules</ital>. There is no justification set out in the <ital>Regulatory Impact Assessment</ital> as to why a retrospective application of the <ital>Rules</ital> is warranted.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Schedule (Rule 9)</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>22</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>It is recommended that the word “counsel” be replaced with authorized representative. The use of the word counsel infuses uncertainty in the <ital>Rule</ital> as it is a term that is not defined and can have many meanings to different audiences, including vulnerable appellants who may be preyed upon by unscrupulous actors.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Additional Recommendation – Multiple issue Appeals</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>23</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The <ital>Rules</ital> should have the flexibility to contemplate/provide notice of additional grounds of inadmissibility that are evident on the record or arise as “de novo” evidence is presented in the IAD process. If additional grounds can be dealt with at the earliest possible instance, this could assist in reducing appeals and facilitate earlier resolution in cases where the additional issue is determinative.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Additional Recommendation - Self Representation and Underrepresentation</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>24</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Self representation and underrepresentation pose serious challenges and can needlessly expend precious resources. Rewriting the rules in plain language can assist both self represented applicants and authorized representatives. It is equally important that appellants who do not have to be self represented do not enter the process without legal assistance or are underrepresented because they could not make an informed decision about hiring counsel. This begins with messaging. There is no direct link to the selection of counsel for appellants searching on the IRB website. The information that can be found under “Frequently Asked Questions” is not sufficient.</bold><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">5</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (23 November 2021). “Learn about Immigration and Citizenship Representatives.” <ital>Government of Canada</ital>, <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="I235dcb807a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45">https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigration-citizenship-representative/learn-about-representatives.html</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Although the aim to protect the public through this messaging is important and appropriate, the result is a severely distorted image with little mention of the critical role authorized representatives play. This fuels a perception that accessing representation is always a perilous decision. The stakes of this public portrayal now are even higher with the increasing reliance on techno-solutions as the technology can further distance the public from the decision-maker.</bold></para.text><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>As we move to a “plain language approach” in the <ital>Rules,</ital> the IRB website should properly portray authorized representatives, the distinctions between representatives, properly highlight qualifications and expertise, and convey to readers to obtain information and guidance. Proper links should be offered to avoid underrepresentation and/or unregulated representation. The IRB website should place the onus on the appellants to make an independent decision about hiring an authorized representative with a balanced presentation of how they can and cannot assist.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Additional Recommendation – IAD Legal Resource Content</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>25</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The legal resources on the IAD website are an important source of information for appellants and authorized representatives alike. It is critical that this information remain current. It should also be expanded. Information provided should include:</bold></para.text></para><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>a</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Up to date changes;</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>b</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Subscription run;</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>c</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Relevant Acts, Regulations, Directions, Gazette Notices, legislative and non-legislative instruments, Forms, and relevant internal policy (disclosable);</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>d</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Tracking updates and access to historical legislative frameworks; and</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0"><bold>e</bold></designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>More effective search facility and hyperlinks connecting relevant information/ legislation to ensure user friendliness.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The Australian Immigration system currently uses a database entitled Legend.com. We understand from lawyers who have worked in that system that it provides a consolidated and centralized source of all up to date policy, legislation, and relevant case law. It is recommended the IAD, and by extension the IRB, investigate a similar option.</bold></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">While much of the feedback provided appears to have been reflected in the new <ital>IAD Rules</ital>, which came into force on 14 January 2023, some was not. For example, while the suggestion to include “in the interests of justice” in s. 3 as an identifiable legal test employed to resolving appeals was not included, s. 2 states: “<ital>These Rules are to be interpreted and applied so as to permit the resolution of every appeal as informally and quickly as the circumstances and the considerations of fairness and natural justice permit.</ital>” The IRB's <ital>Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement</ital> addressed this, noting the IRB “<ital>feels that the Act and the IAD Rules adequately require consideration of fairness and natural justice and therefore no additions are necessary</ital>.”<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">6</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Government of Canada, “Immigration Appeal Division Rules, 2022: SOR/2022-277”, online: <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="I235e19a07a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45">https://www.gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p2/2023/2023-01-04/html/sor-dors277-eng.html</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">As well, the proposition to clarify s.11 of the <ital>IAD Rules</ital> with respect to situations where a conflict of interest arises and a representative may not be able to provide a written request to be removed, was not adopted. Neither was the suggestion to remove the qualifier “relevant” from ss. 20(1)(d), 20(3)(c), or 20(4)(b) to make it necessary for the Minister to disclose <underscore>all</underscore> information pertaining to the matter, rather than simply information they deem “relevant.” The hope, with the latter suggestion, was that this would assist in expediting proceedings further, as appellants would not have to resort to requesting the entirety of their records through <ital>Access to Information and Privacy Requests</ital> (ATIPS) to confirm that all information is before the IAD. However, the IRB explained its decision to keep the word “relevant” in the <ital>IAD Rules</ital>:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>One respondent recommended removing the term “relevant” as a qualifier to the documents the Minister is required to include in an appeal record. The IRB has decided to keep this term in the IAD Rules because a qualifier is needed to avoid having unrelated immigration records disclosed, which would create inefficiencies in the appeal process. It would also result in having more information about the appellant or applicant, potentially involving more sensitive immigration or refugee matters, put into the public realm when it is not material to the appeal.</bold><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">7</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Government of Canada, “Immigration Appeal Division Rules, 2022: SOR/2022-277”, online: <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="I235e40b07a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45">https://www.gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p2/2023/2023-01-04/html/sor-dors277-eng.html</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">However, we are pleased to observe the feedback that has been reflected in the new <ital>IAD Rules</ital>. For example, it was suggested that s. 1 of the <ital>IAD Rules</ital> which defines certain terms used throughout provide clarity on terms such as “in writing” or “written request” be defined and include electronic filing. This has been reflected in the new <ital>IAD Rules</ital> in s. 35-40, which now recognizes that documents may now be provided to the IAD by email or other electronic means, that an electronic document provided is considered the original and considers the time of receipt of an electronic document to be “<ital>on the date and time indicated by the electronic means used to provide it.</ital>”</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This is important and reflects the reality of working in an area of law which has made a major and dramatic shift to fully online or hybrid work, and also makes it more efficient to file and serve documents. Pre-COVID-19 pandemic, most documents needed to be served either in-person, by mail, or by fax which if not adds additional financial cost to filing documents can be more time-consuming and unreliable (i.e., in times where the IAD facsimile line is busy if another individual is attempting to file or send correspondence through facsimile). Having the ability to communicate electronically, in real time, saves on cost, time, and can allow individuals to ensure that their correspondence was received (or not) immediately, and ensure access to justice as not all individuals, especially those that are self-represented in appeals, have access to a fax machine, process-server, etc.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Three further changes were made in line with two of Bellissimo Law Group PC's points outlined above, reflected in the <ital>Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement</ital>:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>The IRB made changes to the prepublished IAD Rules based on the comments received. The changes are as follows:</bold></para.text><list list.style="block" date.updated="0"><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Increasing the time limit to disclose documents from 45 to 60 days after a party receives the appeal record and updating the factors to consider when deciding whether to allow disclosure when the time limit is not met. In addition to the relevance of the document and whether it could have reasonably been provided within the time limits, the factors now also include the prejudice to the other party, the timeliness of the request, and the justification for any delay. These changes were made to respond to concerns that 45 days was not sufficient time to provide disclosure and the recommendation that the disclosure time limit be tied to the hearing date.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Changing the time limit to provide witness information from 45 days after a party receives the appeal record to 30 days before the hearing. Two respondents suggested this change because it would be impractical to submit a list of witnesses when the hearing date is unknown, which may result in overinclusive lists.</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>[…]</bold></para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">•</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>Permitting a party to request a conference under Rule 72 and not just at the Division's own initiative. One comment was made to suggest this addition to support informal resolution and hearing efficiency. The IRB agreed.</bold><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">8</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Government of Canada, “Immigration Appeal Division Rules, 2022: SOR/2022-277”, online: <cite finder="manual" type="url"><ref normalpub="webref" ref.id="I235e67c07a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45">https://www.gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p2/2023/2023-01-04/html/sor-dors277-eng.html</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para></list.item></list></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In all, the new <ital>IAD Rules</ital> are a welcome change to the procedures employed during the appeal process, as they now transfer the focus from preparing for the formal hearing process and allow for pre-hearing, early resolution, earlier in the process. This is to the benefit of all parties: the fewer the appeals that proceed to a full hearing, the less hearings that need to be scheduled, and for which need to be prepared. The earlier in the process the matter is resolved, the sooner an appellant and others impacted by the decision will have a resolution. Further, this means less resources need to be expended on legal representation, allowing more room for options even for appellants to self-represent in the less formal aspects of the appeal process such as early resolution and ADR.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">This, in all, also allows for more matters to move through the appeal process, allowing greater access to justice. Though the new <ital>IAD Rules</ital> have only come into effect approximately six months prior to the date of writing, in practice we are already seeing the positive benefits of the amendments play out, as a greater number of appeals have been resolved early without the need to proceed to a full hearing. These new rules are certainly a step in the right direction in allowing appeals to be processed with increased fairness and efficiency. We are very pleased the IAD was so receptive to feedback reflective of a meaningful consultation process.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:28: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division</value><value>IMM.IV.2.j Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Inadmissible classes—Misrepresentation</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:28</designator><name date.updated="0">Removal Order Appeals in Misrepresentation Cases</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">IAD Members have the jurisdiction to consider stay requests in misrepresentation removal order cases. While the granting of stays is discretionary, there have been cases where stays have been granted with varied conditions even where the misrepresentations were deemed to be grave. For example, in <ital>Lin</ital>, <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>Lin v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)</ital> (October 2, 2014), Doc. 5239-0138, T83-01023 (Can. I.R.B.), at paras. 122–123; see also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Mohammad" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)" post.rptr="5725" pre.rptr="2003" ref.id="I94bd22609b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Mohammad v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)">Mohammad v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2003 CarswellNat 5725</ref></cite>, at para. 24; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Ryan" p2="Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)" post.rptr="8221" pre.rptr="2011" ref.id="I94bd22619b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Ryan v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)">Ryan v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2011 CarswellNat 8221,</ref></cite> at para. 20; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Patel" p2="Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)" post.rptr="8277" pre.rptr="2013" ref.id="I94bd22629b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Patel v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)">Patel v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 CarswellNat 8277</ref></cite>, at para. 10.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> the IAD determined it was inappropriate to allow the appeal and instead put the applicant on a five-year stay due to the seriousness of the appellant's misrepresentation and her lack of genuine remorse. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">2</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">The IAD went on to state that “Her conduct displays a continuing and deliberate intention to mislead. A lengthy stay will give her an opportunity to gain genuine and sincere remorse with respect to her misrepresentation and to demonstrate that she can be a law-abiding resident of Canada and have respect for the integrity of Canada's immigration system.”</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Therefore, stay orders are being applied in misrepresentation removal cases but with a cautionary note. In <ital>Yao</ital>, <footnote date.trace="20231124" date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="20231124">3-4</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Yao and Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), Re" post.rptr="4427" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I94bd49709b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Yao and Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), Re">Yao and Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), Re, 2017 CarswellNat 4427 (Imm. & Ref. Bd. (App. Div.))</ref></cite>, at para 14.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> for example, the IAD denied the stay, harshly criticizing the appellant for requesting a stay, stating that</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>In the face of such damage to our immigration system, the idea that a stay of the appeal and “hundreds” of hours of community service could be an appropriate thing to ask for reflects a lack of a real grasp of the magnitude of the seriousness of his misrepresentation. His actions have drained finite resources and brought the integrity of Canada's immigration system into disrepute, and each case of misrepresentation, as mentioned, brings greater scrutiny to law-abiding applicants, slowing down the processing time. Asking for a stay misses the point, to think that the damage done can now be quantified. Community service cannot make up for that. The fact that he does not see that shows that he does not think what he did was a wrong as it was. And in misrepresentation cases, since the goal of permanent residence has already been achieved, there is no point in re-offending. That also makes a stay inappropriate.</bold></para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">This raises the question of whether a stay of removal in misrepresentation cases will be an exceptional finding. A crucial distinction may be drawn between post-admission criminal conduct, where there has been a valid and legitimate initial admission decision, and misrepresentation that occurs during the initial admission process to Canada. Family sponsorship-related cases involving misrepresentation often fall into the latter cases.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">In cases where there are compelling humanitarian considerations, including a strong family nucleus in Canada and the best interests of the child as well as potential mitigating factors surrounding the original misrepresentation, it may be appropriate to grant a stay of removal. It is worth noting that the IAD has also found that where a stay was not appropriate, the panel allowed the appeal and set aside the removal order. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">5</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Salvana" p2="Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)" post.rptr="64605" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I94bd49719b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Salvana v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)">Salvana v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2017 CanLII 64605; <ital>Sharma and Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), Re</ital>, 2017 CarswellNat 5330</ref></cite>.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">As such, it would appear that a stay request in misrepresentation removal order cases is available and appropriate for certain cases but will not easily be granted and the applicability of such a request may continue to linger in the minds of certain IAD members. This will be an interesting aspect of appeals involving inadmissibility based on misrepresentation to follow.</para.text></para></section.body></section>
10:29: <section date.revised="0" date.updated="0"><metadata.block metadata.store="yes"><metadata field="classification"><value>IMM.IV.5.g.i Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Removal from Canada—Appeals and judicial review—Immigration Appeal Division</value><value>IMM.IV.2.j Immigration and citizenship—Exclusion and removal—Inadmissible classes—Misrepresentation</value></metadata></metadata.block><section.front date.updated="0"><outline.name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><label date.updated="0">§</label><designator date.updated="0">10:29</designator><name date.updated="0">The Five-Year Bar and the Retrospective Application of the Two-Year Bar in Misrepresentation Cases</name></outline.name.block></section.front><section.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">Amendments to s. 40(2)(a) of the <ital>IRPA</ital> came into force on 20 November 2014 as a result of the <ital>Faster Removal of Foreign Criminals Act (FRFCA)</ital>, following which the inadmissibility period associated with findings of misrepresentation was raised from two years to five years. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">1</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>Immigration and Refugee Protection Act</ital>, S.C. 2001, c. 27, ss. 40(1)(a), 40(2) [20 November 2014]; <ital>Immigration and Refugee Protection Act</ital>, S.C. 2001, c. 27, ss. 40(1)(a), 40(2) [current]; <ital>Faster Removal of Foreign Criminals Act</ital>, S.C. 2013, c. 16, s. 16 [<ital>FRFCA</ital>].</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> A previously publicly-available Operation Bulletin 595 (OB 595), obtained by way of an <ital>Access to Information and Privacy</ital> request, outlines the CBSA and IRCC interpretation of the change in law. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">2</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Canada, Immigration, Refugees, and Citizenship Canada, <ital>Coming into force of Bill C-43: misrepresentation increased from two to five years for temporary and permanent residents</ital>, Operational Bulletin 595 (November 28, 2014).</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> According to OB 595, the new, five-year period of inadmissibility is applicable as of the date a removal order is enforced. Thus, even if an individual was issued a removal order for misrepresentation prior to 20 November 2014, based upon the OB they would be subject to the new, five-year period of inadmissibility wherever the order is enforced on or after 21 November 2014. However, OB 595 does not have the force of law and may well reflect an incorrect interpretation of the <ital>IRPA</ital>. On this issue, we turn to the language of the Act, case law, and relevant interpretive principles.</para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="20231124">The IAD has been uneven in its application as to whether the two-year or the five-year bar would apply if the appellant's appeal is dismissed. The provision addresses when the inadmissibility period begins, rather than specifying that the duration of inadmissibility is calculated as of when the removal order is enforced. It remains to be determined whether the cases (between 2013–2014) straddling the time period during which the amendments came into force could benefit from the two-year ban, or if the five-year ban applies retrospectively to these cases. The IAD has only addressed this issue in a few cases and at that, inconsistently. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">3</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">See e.g., <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Abdallah" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)" post.rptr="5768" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I94bd70809b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Abdallah v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)">Abdallah v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 CarswellNat 5768</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Yu" p2="Canada (P.S.E.P.)" post.rptr="97776" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I94bd70819b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Yu v. Canada (P.S.E.P.)">Yu v. Canada (P.S.E.P.), 2015 CanLII 97776</ref></cite>; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Cai" p2="Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)" post.rptr="7913" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I94bd70829b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Cai v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)">Cai v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2015 CarswellNat 7913</ref></cite>, at para 20; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Chen" p2="Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)" post.rptr="12173" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I94bd70839b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Chen v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)">Chen v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2015 CarswellNat 12173</ref></cite>, paras. 12, 22, 25; <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Xu" p2="Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)" post.rptr="9398" pre.rptr="2015" ref.id="I94bd97909b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Xu v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)">Xu v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2015 CarswellNat 9398</ref></cite>. Note that in these cases, there is no indication that Parliament intended the new inadmissibility period to have retroactive effect.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.trace="20231124" date.updated="20231124"><para.text date.updated="0">However, the Federal Court has weighed in on this issue in the decision of <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Zeng" p2="Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)" post.rptr="1586" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I235f79307a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45" title="Zeng v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)">Zeng v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1586 (F.C.)</ref></cite>, where Justice McHaffie determined that the two-year inadmissibility period applied to the applicant where the IAD had issued an exclusion order before the amendments to the law but was enforced after that date.<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">3.10</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">See <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Zeng" p2="Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)" post.rptr="1586" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I235f79317a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45" title="Zeng v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)">Zeng v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1586 (F.C.)</ref></cite> at paras. 1-4.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> After conducting a review and analysis of OB 595, considering principles of statutory interpretation, retroactivity and retrospectivity, Justice McHaffie concluded applying the five-year inadmissibility period to an individual found inadmissible for misrepresentation and subject to removal before 21 November 2014 “<ital>would amount to retrospective application of the amendments to section 40 of the</ital> IRPA.”<footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">3.20</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">See <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Zeng" p2="Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)" post.rptr="1586" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I235fa0407a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45" title="Zeng v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)">Zeng v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1586 (F.C.)</ref></cite> at paras. 24-44.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> In wrapping up the discussion of the issue, the Court concluded:</para.text><quote.block date.updated="0"><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>[51] In the absence of any legislative indication that the amendments to section 40 enacted by the FRFCA were intended to apply retrospectively, I conclude that the inadmissibility period imposed by an exclusion order for misrepresentation prior to November 21, 2014 continues to be two years, whether or not the exclusion order was enforced before or after that date.</bold></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>[52] I note that on a strict application of the principles in Tran, one might conclude that the two-year inadmissibility period should apply whenever the misrepresentation occurred prior to the change in the legislation, considering that to be equivalent to the “time of the commission of the offence”: Tran at paras 35-41.</bold></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>[53] I do not need to decide this issue in this case, as both Mr. Zeng's misrepresentation and the resulting exclusion order predated the amendments. However, there are two primary reasons that I do not believe this to be the correct interpretation. First, in Tran, Justice Côté recognized that the triggering language in the IRPA was the date of conviction, rather than the date of commission of the offence. It was only the operation of subsection 11(i) of the Charter that in turn made the date of commission of the offence relevant, since the maximum sentence imposable on conviction is that in place at the time of the offence: Tran at paras 36-38. Second, a misrepresentation may not be discovered for many years, which would result in both a potentially lengthy “transition” period and an unnecessary debate over when a misrepresentation occurred. The date of the exclusion order that imposes the inadmissibility consequence sets a clear date for assessing the length of the consequence, even though enforcement may not occur until some time later. The concern regarding retrospectivity is therefore attenuated.</bold></para.text></quote.para><quote.para pstart="n" date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><bold>[54] If I were required to decide the issue, I would therefore conclude that the relevant date for assessing the applicable inadmissibility period for misrepresentation is the date of the exclusion order, rather than the date of the misrepresentation. In other words, exclusion orders issued on or after November 21, 2014 impose a consequence of inadmissibility that continues for a period of five years from the date of enforcement; those issued prior to November 21, 2014 impose a consequence of inadmissibility that continues for a period of two years from the date of enforcement.</bold><footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">3.30</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">See <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Zeng" p2="Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)" post.rptr="1586" pre.rptr="2019" ref.id="I235fc7507a3c11eeae2bcd9e4a381e45" title="Zeng v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)">Zeng v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1586 (F.C.)</ref></cite> at paras. 51-54.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></quote.para></quote.block></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">It is submitted that the new, more severe penalty would not apply to applicants who are issued a removal order prior to the FRFCA coming into force. There is a presumption against the retrospective or retroactive operation of statutes, unless expressly required by the language of the act. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">4</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="British Columbia" p2="Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd." post.rptr="49" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I94bd97919b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.">British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2005 SCC 49, [2005] 2 S.C.R. 473 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, at para. 69 [<ital>Imperial Tobacco</ital>]; see also <cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Tran" p2="Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)" post.rptr="50" pre.rptr="2017" ref.id="I94bd97929b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Tran v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness)">Tran v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2017 SCC 50 (S.C.C.)</ref></cite>, at para. 43.</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> The presumption against retrospectivity is not concerned only with punishment or penal consequences, and this principle has been similarly applied in the immigration context. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">5</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><cite finder="manual" type="case"><ref p1="Singh" p2="Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)" post.rptr="417" pre.rptr="2005" ref.id="I94bd97939b8911eba00cf959916bd810" title="Singh v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration)">Singh v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship & Immigration), 2005 FCA 417 (F.C.A.)</ref></cite>, at para. 33 [<ital>Singh</ital>].</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote> As such, Parliament likely did not desire the retrospective application of the five-year inadmissibility period to cases of misrepresentation when amending the <ital>IRPA</ital> between 2013 and 2014. Neither the <ital>FRFCA</ital> nor the <ital>Order</ital> contain transitional provisions or otherwise address the issue of whether the more severe misrepresentation penalty applies to removal orders issued before the coming into force of the modified s. 40(1)(a) of the <ital>IRPA</ital> in November 2014. <ital>Hansard</ital> notes are also silent on this particular issue. <footnote date.updated="0"><footnote.reference date.updated="0">6</footnote.reference><footnote.body date.updated="0"><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0"><ital>Standing Senate Committee on Social Affairs, Science and Technology</ital>, Evidence, 1st Sess., 41st Parl., Meetings No. 1, 2; 1, 2 May 2013 at 38:19 and 38:61 (Hon. Jason Kenney, P.C., M.P., Minister, Citizenship and Immigration; Hon. Senator Seidman).</para.text></para></footnote.body></footnote></para.text></para><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Changes in law are presumed to be prospective as, absent clear statutory language, it is presumed that it was not the legislative intent to create new consequences for past actions. As there is no evidence that Parliament intended the increased inadmissibility period to apply retroactively to removal orders issued prior to 20 November 2014, the two-year inadmissibility period in force when the applicant's removal order was issued should apply.</para.text></para></section.body></section>

date.updated="0">Identify issues within the appeal and any other admissibility issues. The objective is to canvass all issues to prevent multiple appeals and refused cases.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">9</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Examine fact-similar case law at both the IAD as well as the Federal Court and beyond including criminal court divisions and understand themes and any interpretative decisions at various judicial levels.</para.text></para></list.item><list.item date.updated="0"><name.block toc.include="y" date.updated="0"><designator date.updated="0">10</designator></name.block><para date.updated="0"><para.text date.updated="0">Consult the Act, the Regulations, the Division Rules, and the Guidelines and do not assume your issue has been decided before.
